This is clear, as we said; it follows the pattern of familiar similes, and its aim is to establish beauty, because He, the Exalted, set in natures that nothing is more beautiful than an angel, and the people of Lūṭ witnessed that in the guests of Ibrāhīm, who were angels, just as He set in natures that nothing is uglier than the devil. Likewise His saying, the Exalted, describing Hell: «طلعها كأنه رؤوس الشيطان». Thus it is established that nothing is more beautiful than an angel, so when the women wished to describe Yūsuf as beautiful, they likened him to an angel. But the Qur'anic style willed to go beyond the familiar in the Arabs' similes, who compare to the jinn everything of human beauty that amazed them, so it brought into it another art that does not appear to the viewer at first glance. It is the art they knew as the speaker's asking about what he truly knows, feigning ignorance, so that his speech comes out as praise, or to indicate, as here, the intensity of passion in love; it may also be intended for blame, wonder, rebuke or confirmation. This art is called tajāhul al-ʿārif ("feigned ignorance of the one who knows"), and it is of two kinds: affirmative and negative.
A- The affirmative:
It is that in which the question is about two things, one of which has occurred and the other has not, and the speaker may pronounce one and be silent about the other because the situation indicates it. Of this chapter is His saying, the Exalted: «أبشرا منا واحدا نتبعه», which comes out as wonder, and its discussion will come when we reach this verse in Sūrat al-Qamar; and His saying, the Exalted: «قالوا يا شعيب أصلاتك تأمرك أن نترك ما يبعد آباؤنا أو أن نفعل في أموالنا ما نشاء», which comes out as rebuke and was mentioned in Sūrat Hūd; and His saying, the Exalted: «أأنت فعلت هذا بآلهتنا يا إبراهيم», which comes out as confirmation. All of it is affirmative, as you have seen.
B- The negative:
As for the verse we are concerned with, it is of the negative kind. The simile went beyond, as we said, the Arabs' likening to the jinn of everyone whose beauty amazed them, to the likening of Yūsuf, when his beauty was manifestly awe-inspiring, surpassing in its radiance and comeliness the familiar, customary wonders of beauty. With his evident splendour he had light and awe, openness and radiance, and over him was a touch of tranquillity that reassured the one who looked at him against that awe and steadied his heart through the tranquillity that flowed into it, a sign of good, and an allure toward what holds the soul's ease and delight. So his likening to the noble angel was thus.
The simile protected from banality:
Since our talk has drawn us into these matters where the craft is subtle and its secrets are hidden except from the inspired who have tasted the secrets of the people, we cannot avoid pointing out that this art is resorted to in the simile in a special way, to depart from imitation, to raise the simile to the farthest horizons and to protect it from banality. Had the verse not presented the likening of Yūsuf to the angel in this style, preceded by the negation that requires strangeness, the simile would not have had that fine effect. Of this is the saying of the poet of immortality, al-Mutanabbī:
لم تلق هذا الوجه شمس نهارنا ... إلا بوجه ليس فيه حياء
(Our daytime sun does not meet this face except with a face that has no shame in it.)
He meant to liken the face to the sun, but this simile is so common that, through its commonness, it nearly sinks to the depth of banality; so he wished to protect it by putting a feigned negation before it, saying: there is no need of the sun with your brightness and your light, but in its impudence it rises upon you.
Feigned ignorance in poetry:
Tajāhul al-ʿārif has an effect on the souls like the grip of magic and the intoxication of wine; therefore al-Sakkākī, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "I do not like to call it 'feigned ignorance', because it occurs often in the speech of Allah the Exalted." Then he gave it another name: "driving what is known along the course of something else, for a subtle point." Our poetry overflows with it, and it is not limited to praise or love poetry, as we said, but passes beyond them to any exaggeration in any of the themes that occur to minds. Listen to the saying of Zuhayr ibn Abī Sulmā and you will see a wonder of wonders. He said, satirising Ḥiṣn ibn Ḥudhayfa al-Fazārī:
وما أدري وسوف إخال أدري ... أقوم آل حصن أم نساء
(I do not know, and I shall soon think I know, whether the family of Ḥiṣn are men or women.)
See how it occurred to him to deny knowledge of the state of the family, then, before completing that, it occurred to him to assert firmly that he would know, then, before completing that, he said that attaining knowledge in the future is by way of imagination and supposition; so he related the state of the soul in its hesitation about the matter.
And I am delighted by the saying of Abū al-ʿAbbās al-Nāmī:
أحقا أن قاتلتي زرود ... وأن عهودها تلك العهود
وقفت وقد فقدت الصبر حتى ... تبين موقفي أني الفقيد
وشكك فيّ عذالي فقالوا ... لرسم الدار أيكما العميد؟
(Is it true that my killer is Zarūd, and that her pledges are those pledges? I stood, having lost patience, until my standing made clear that I was the one lost. My blamers made doubt of me and said to the ruins of the abode: which of you two is the one stricken?)
And the cry of Ibn al-Rūmī, the cry of bewilderment when he sees the red cheek beside the jet-black temple-lock:
يا وجنتيه اللتين من بهج ... فيّ صدغييه اللذين من دعج ما حمرة فيكما؟ أمن خجل ... أم صبغة الله أم دم المهج
[Translator's note: the two verses are run together in the source, and the second half of the first verse and the opening of the second are mixed; translated as they stand.]
(O his two cheeks, of delight, and his two temples, of deep blackness: what is the redness in you? Is it from shyness, or the dye of Allah, or the blood of hearts?)
And Laylā bint Ṭarīf the Khārijite composed a fine verse in lamenting her brother:
أيا شجر الخابور مالك مورقا ... كأنك لم تجزع على ابن طريف
(O trees of the Khābūr, why are you in leaf, as if you did not grieve over Ibn Ṭarīf?)
And Mihyār wished to liken the beloved to the gazelle, the full moon and the branch of the ban tree, so he passed beyond the familiar and customary, and rose to a sky that no sky rivals, when he said:
سلا ظبية الوادي وما الظبي مثلها ... وإن كان مصقول الترائب أكحلا
أأنت أمرت البدر أن يصدع الدجى ... وعلمت غصن البان أن يتميّلا
(Ask the gazelle of the valley, though the gazelle is not like her, even if it is polished of breast and kohl-eyed: did you command the full moon to split the darkness, and teach the branch of the ban to sway?)
We close this delightful chapter with the saying of al-Bahāʾ Zuhayr:
رعى الله ليلة وصل خلت ... وما خالط الصفو فيها الكدر
أتت بغتة ومضت سرعة ... وما قصرت بعد ذاك القصر
بغير احتيال ولا كلفة ... ولا موعد بيننا ينتظر
فقلت وقد كاد عقلي يطير ... سرورا بنيل المنى والوطر
أيا قلب تعرف من قد أتاك ... ويا عين تدرين من قد حضر
ويا قمر الأفق عد راجعا ... فقد حل في الدار عندي القمر
ويا ليلتي هكذا هكذا ... وبالله قف يا سحر فكانت كما أشتهي ليلة ... وطاب الحديث وطاب ا
لسهر خلونا وما بيننا ثالث ... فأصبح عند النسيم الخبر
(May Allah watch over a night of union that passed, with no turbidity mixed into its clarity. It came suddenly and passed quickly, and it did not fall short after that shortness. Without contrivance or effort, and without an appointment awaited between us. I said, my mind almost flying with joy at attaining wishes and needs: O heart, do you know who has come to you? O eye, do you know who is present? O moon of the horizon, return, for the moon has alighted in the house with me. O my night, thus, thus; by Allah, stay, O dawn! It was a night as I desire, the talk was sweet and the waking was sweet; we were alone with no third between us, and at the breeze the news spread.)
[Translator's note: the source text is broken at "وطاب ا / لسهر"; it is reproduced as it stands.]
And al-Sharīf al-Raḍī says, which is the utmost of utmosts:
بين الاظاعن حاجة خلفتها ... أودعتها يوم الفراق مودعي
وأظنها لا بل يقيني انها ... قلبي لأني لم أجد قلبي معي
(Among the departing there is a need I left behind, which I deposited on the day of parting with my farewell-giver. I think it, no, I am certain, that it is my heart, for I do not find my heart with me.)

2- Omission:
In His saying «فذلكن الذي لمتنني فيه», the implied form is "in his love", because blame is not attached to persons. The evidence for the implied "in his love" is His saying «قد شغفها حبا»; or "in soliciting him", and perhaps this is preferable, by the evidence of His saying: «تراود فتاها عن نفسه». We said it is preferable because it was her act, unlike love, which is an overpowering matter for which one is blamed only in respect of pursuing its causes. As for soliciting, it occurs through her own acquiring, so she is able to ward it off, and blame can attach to it, unlike love, which is not her act and which she cannot ward off, since excessive love may overpower its owner so that he cannot repel it, and then he is not blamed for it; in any case it is among its causes.
3- In His saying «متكأ» there is a depiction of a kind of food that is only served for relish, ease, adornment of the gathering and abundance of the means of enjoyment in it, so much so that the custom is that one turns to it in a state of rest and reclining. The word, moreover, is one of the many words whose formation the Qur'an created beautifully, and which the Arabs later took up; had it not been for that, they would not have found their way to them, and the language would have failed them in this area in depicting what they wanted. Look when the Qur'an describes the wife of al-ʿAzīz's invitation of the women who had been talking critically of her soliciting Yūsuf, to a delightful, splendid sitting in her house, to show them Yūsuf and his beauty so that they would excuse her for what she had undertaken. She served them food in that gathering, no doubt, and the Qur'an made this clear, but it did not express it with "food"; for that word only depicts the desire of hunger and carries the mind to the "kitchen" with all its varieties of food, its smells and its means.

* Benefits:
1- (حاشا) occurs in three ways:
1- As a transitive, inflected verb. You say حاشيته meaning "I excepted him", and if ما precedes it, it is negative.
2- For exoneration, as in حاشا لله, in which case it is a noun synonymous with التنزيه ("exoneration"), in the accusative as an absolute object. It is also said to be a verb, and the alif is retained and dropped.
3- It may be for exception, in which case it is a particle in the position of إلا, except that it puts the excepted in the genitive. There are other details to be consulted in the longer works.

2- The difference between the two nūns of emphasis:
The majority of the Basrans hold that the heavy and the light nūn of emphasis are both original, because of their difference in some of their rules, such as the substitution of the light by alif in the like of وليكونا, and its dropping in the like of the poet's words:
ولا تهين الفقير علك أن ... تركع يوما والدهر قد رفعه
(Do not humiliate the poor man; perhaps you will bow one day, while time has raised him.)
and both are impossible with the heavy nūn. This is what Sībawayh said, and it was countered that the derived may sometimes have what the original does not; Sībawayh himself said regarding أن (with fatḥa) that it is derived from the kasra form (إنّ), and it has, when lightened, rules particular to it. As for the Kufans, they hold that the light is derived from the heavy.
Al-Khalīl ibn Aḥmad mentioned that emphasis with the heavy is stronger than emphasis with the light, as indicated by «ليسجنن وليكونن»: the wife of al-ʿAzīz was more eager for his imprisonment than for his being humiliated.
3- The elative stripped of al and of annexation does not, in most cases, lack a sharing of meaning with that which is surpassed, in wording or in implication. By "in implication" we mean a sharing in some respect, as in their saying about two hated things: هذا أحب إلي من هذا ("this is dearer to me than that"), and about two evils: هذا خير من هذا ("this is better than that"); and in the Revelation: «قال رب السجن أحب إلي مما يدعونني إليه». The interpretation of that is "this is less hateful and less evil". Of the non-predominant case: العسل أحلى من الخل ("honey is sweeter than vinegar") and الصيف آخر من الشتاء ("summer is later than winter").

dervis-irab:7-14.t:
* Vocabulary:
(غَيابَتِ الْجُبِّ): al-ghayāba is a covering or an arch in a well near the water, which hides what is in it from the eyes. Al-Zamakhsharī said: it is its depth, and what of it is hidden from the eye of the observer and is dark at its bottom. Al-Munakhkhal said:
إذا أنا يوما غيبتني غيابتي ... فسيروا بسيري في العشيرة والأهل
(If one day my ghayāba hides me, then go about as I used to go among the clan and the family.) He meant the ghayāba of his grave, in which he is buried. Al-jubb is the well that has not been lined with stone. It is so called either because it is dug in the "pockets" of the earth, that is, its thick parts, or because it is cut into the earth; its plural is ajbāb, jibāb and jababa.
(السَّيَّارَةِ): plural of sayyār, that is, one who is excessive in travelling. In al-Mukhtār: "al-sayyāra is the caravan." So their calling the well-known vehicle of today "al-sayyāra" is correct and beyond reproach, because it is the feminine of sayyār.

* I'rab:
(لَقَدْ كانَ فِي يُوسُفَ وَإِخْوَتِهِ آياتٌ لِلسَّائِلِينَ) The lām is the response to an omitted oath; قد is a particle of confirmation; كان is a defective past verb; في يوسف is a fronted khabar; إخوته is conjoined to يوسف; آيات is the postponed noun of كان; and للسائلين is an adjective of آيات. (إِذْ قالُوا: لَيُوسُفُ وَأَخُوهُ أَحَبُّ إِلى أَبِينا مِنَّا) إذ is an adverbial of past time attached to an omitted verb, its implied form being "اذكر" (remember); it is also said that the adverbial is attached to كان. The clause قالوا is what the adverbial is annexed to. The lām is the lām of ibtidāʾ (inception), and in it is an emphasis confirming the content of the sentence. أخوه is conjoined to يوسف, and he is Binyāmīn, his full brother. أحب is the khabar; إلى أبينا is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to أحب. It has already been stated that when the elative (afʿal al-tafḍīl) or the two forms of wonder (afʿil bihi, mā afʿalahu) are formed from "love" and "hatred", the verb from them is made transitive to the semantic agent by إلى and to the semantic object by the lām; so if you say زيد أحب إلي من بكر, its meaning is that you love Zayd more than Bakr. منا is likewise attached to أحب. أحب does not agree in the dual, because the elative is obligatorily singular and masculine when it is accompanied by من; a distinction is necessary with الـ, and when it is annexed both are permissible. «[Translator's note: the source's "a distinction is necessary with al" is rendered as written; it means that with the definite article the elative must agree in number and gender.]» (وَنَحْنُ عُصْبَةٌ إِنَّ أَبانا لَفِي ضَلالٍ مُبِينٍ) The wāw is the wāw of ḥāl; نحن is a mubtadaʾ and عصبة its khabar; inna and its noun; the shifted lām (al-lām al-muzaḥlaqa); في ضلال is its khabar; and مبين is an adjective. Al-ʿuṣba is a group; it is said: it is what is between one and ten. (اقْتُلُوا يُوسُفَ أَوِ اطْرَحُوهُ أَرْضاً يَخْلُ لَكُمْ وَجْهُ أَبِيكُمْ) اقتلوا is an imperative verb, the wāw is the fāʿil, and يوسف is a mafʿūl bihi; أو اطرحوه is conjoined to اقتلوا; and أرضا is put in the accusative with the accusative of vague adverbials, that is, an unknown, unfamiliar land far from habitation. Al-Zamakhsharī said, and Ibn ʿAṭiyya said: "That is a mistake, because the adverbial must be vague, and this is not so; rather it is a land restricted by being far or remote and the like, so its vagueness has gone; and it is known that Yūsuf was never without being in some land, so it is clear that they meant a far land other than the one he was in, near his father." Abū Ḥayyān upheld this refutation.
It is also permissible for it to be accusative by removal of the preposition, that is, "in a land" (في أرض), with the sense of an adverbial; and it is said: it is a second object of اطرحوه, which includes the meaning of "set him down" (أنزلوه). يخل is the response to the imperative; لكم is attached to يخل; وجه is the fāʿil and أبيكم a muḍāf ilayhi. The meaning of يخل لكم وجه أبيكم will come in the section on Rhetoric. (وَتَكُونُوا مِنْ بَعْدِهِ قَوْماً صالِحِينَ) وتكونوا is conjoined to يخل; the wāw is the noun of كان; من بعده is a ḥāl; قوما is the khabar and صالحين an adjective. (قالَ قائِلٌ مِنْهُمْ لا تَقْتُلُوا يُوسُفَ وَأَلْقُوهُ فِي غَيابَتِ الْجُبِّ) قال قائل is a verb and agent, and منهم is an adjective; لا is prohibitive; تقتلوا is an imperfect verb, jussive by لا, the wāw is the fāʿil, and يوسف is a mafʿūl bihi; ألقوه is an imperative verb, agent and direct object; and في غيابة الجب is attached to ألقوه. (يَلْتَقِطْهُ بَعْضُ السَّيَّارَةِ إِنْ كُنْتُمْ فاعِلِينَ) يلتقطه is jussive because it occurs as the response to the imperative; بعض السيارة is the fāʿil; إن is conditional; and كنتم فاعلين is كان with its noun and khabar. The apodosis of إن is omitted, that is, "if you are bent on doing what will achieve the aim", and this is the correct view. (قالُوا يا أَبانا ما لَكَ لا تَأْمَنَّا عَلى يُوسُفَ) قالوا is a verb and agent; يا أبانا is the one addressed, in a muḍāf; ما is an interrogative noun, a mubtadaʾ, and لك is the khabar of ما; لا is negative; تأمنا is an imperfect verb whose fāʿil is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "أنت"; نا is a mafʿūl bihi. The nūn of تأمن has been assimilated into نا, and it has been read in various forms. على يوسف is attached to تأمنا, and the clause لا تأمنا is a ḥāl. The clause مالك لا تأمنا is the content of the saying, and the implied meaning is "what thing is established for you regarding us?" (وَإِنَّا لَهُ لَناصِحُونَ) The wāw is the wāw of ḥāl; inna and its noun; له is attached to ناصحون; the shifted lām; and ناصحون is the khabar of إنا. The clause is a ḥāl from نا, so it is a ḥāl from a ḥāl. (أَرْسِلْهُ مَعَنا غَداً يَرْتَعْ وَيَلْعَبْ وَإِنَّا لَهُ لَحافِظُونَ) أرسله is an imperative verb, with a latent agent and a direct object; معنا is an adverbial of place attached to أرسله, and نا is a muḍāf ilayhi; غدا is an adverbial also attached to أرسله; يرتع is jussive because it is the response to the imperative, and يلعب is conjoined to it. The clause إنا له لحافظون is a ḥāl clause, and its i'rab has already been given. (قالَ إِنِّي لَيَحْزُنُنِي أَنْ تَذْهَبُوا بِهِ) inna and its noun; the shifted lām; the clause يحزنني is the khabar of إنّ, and the yāʾ is a mafʿūl bihi; أن and what is in its scope are in the interpretation of a maṣdar, the fāʿil of يحزنني; and به is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to تذهبوا.
(وَأَخافُ أَنْ يَأْكُلَهُ الذِّئْبُ) أن and what is in its scope is the object of أخاف, and الذئب is the fāʿil of يأكله. Do not let it escape you that he taught them the excuse which they would plead, in line with the proverb "Affliction is entrusted to speech." (وَأَنْتُمْ عَنْهُ غافِلُونَ) The wāw is the wāw of ḥāl; أنتم is a mubtadaʾ and غافلون its khabar; and عنه is attached to غافلون. (قالُوا: لَئِنْ أَكَلَهُ الذِّئْبُ وَنَحْنُ عُصْبَةٌ إِنَّا إِذاً لَخاسِرُونَ) The lām is the one that prepares for an oath; إن is conditional; أكله الذئب is verb, direct object and agent; the wāw is circumstantial, نحن is a mubtadaʾ and عصبة its khabar, and the clause is a ḥāl clause; inna and its noun; إذن is a particle of response and consequence, not operating; and خاسرون is the khabar of إنا. The clause is the response to the oath, and the clause of the apodosis of the condition is omitted, because the response is given to the one that came first, as we established previously.

* Rhetoric:
1- Metaphor (majāz) in His saying, the Exalted: «يخل لكم وجه أبيكم». The face is mentioned only because when a man turns toward something he turns to it with his face, since the first thing that a person faces with is the face; so it expressed by it his turning to them, his not looking to others, and the absence of any partner for them in their father's love.
2- And in His saying «لخاسرون» there is a metaphor for weakness and incapacity; the relation is causality.

dervis-irab:58-62.t:
* I'rab:
(وَجاءَ إِخْوَةُ يُوسُفَ فَدَخَلُوا عَلَيْهِ): the discourse is conjoined to earlier discourse that is understood from the flow of the story, that is: hardship struck Yaʿqūb and his sons while they were in Palestine, so Yaʿqūb said to them: "It has reached me that in Egypt there is a righteous king who sells food, so make ready for him and go to him, that you may buy the food we need." They set out until they reached Egypt ... to the end of the story. وجاء إخوة يوسف: a verb and an agent. Yūsuf is not fully declinable (diptote) because of being a proper name and non-Arabic. فدخلوا عليه: conjoined to وجاء إخوة يوسف.
(فَعَرَفَهُمْ وَهُمْ لَهُ مُنْكِرُونَ): the فاء is a conjunction. عرفهم: a verb, a latent agent and a direct object. The واو is circumstantial. هم: a mubtadaʾ. له: attached to منكرون. منكرون: the khabar; that is, they did not recognise him because of the length of time.
(وَلَمَّا جَهَّزَهُمْ بِجَهازِهِمْ قالَ ائْتُونِي بِأَخٍ لَكُمْ مِنْ أَبِيكُمْ): the واو is a conjunction, and the discourse is conjoined to an implied passage understood from the flow of the dialogue, that is: when they reached him he said to them, "Perhaps you have come as spies to look at the weak points of my country." They said, "Allah forbid! We are a people from the people of al-Shām, shepherds; hardship struck us so we came to get provisions." He asked them to clarify their affair, and they said: "We are brothers, sons of one father, who is an old man, a truthful one, a prophet named Yaʿqūb, and we were twelve, but one of us perished." He said: "You are ten now, so where is the eleventh brother?" They said: "He is with his father, who consoles himself through him for the one lost, because he is his full brother." He said: "Bring him to me," that is, your brother who is from your father, "if you are truthful, and leave one of you with me as a pledge until you bring him to me" ... and so on. لما is temporal or connective. جهزهم: a verb, a latent agent and a direct object. بجهازهم: attached to جهزهم. قال: a clause with no grammatical position because it is the answer to لما. The clause ائتوني is the quoted speech; it is an imperative verb, an agent and a direct object. بأخ: a preposition and its genitive noun attached to it. لكم: an adjective of أخ. من أبيكم: a second adjective.
(أَلا تَرَوْنَ أَنِّي أُوفِي الْكَيْلَ وَأَنَا خَيْرُ الْمُنْزِلِينَ): the hamza is interrogative, and لا negative. ترون: an imperfect verb, nominative by the retention of the nūn, and the wāw is the agent. أن and what follows it take the place of the two objects of ترون. The clause أوفي الكيل is the khabar of أن. The واو is a conjunction. أنا: a mubtadaʾ. خير المنزلين: the khabar, that is, "and I, for the guest, am the best of hosts".
(فَإِنْ لَمْ تَأْتُونِي بِهِ فَلا كَيْلَ لَكُمْ عِنْدِي وَلا تَقْرَبُونِ): the فاء is a conjunction. إن is conditional. لم is a particle of negation, inversion and jussive. تأتوني is jussive through لم, and it is the protasis. The فاء is connective. لا is the lā of generic negation. كيل: its subject. لكم: its khabar. عندي: an adverb attached to an omitted ḥāl. The واو is a conjunction. لا is prohibitive. تقربون: an imperfect verb jussive through لا, its sign of jussive being the dropping of the nūn; this nūn is the nūn of protection (wiqāya), and the first-person yāʾ was dropped for lightness. It is also possible that لا is negative and تقربون is jussive by coordination with the position of his words فلا كيل لكم, which is jussive because it is the apodosis, as though it were said: "if you do not bring him to me you will be deprived and will not come near."
(قالُوا سَنُراوِدُ عَنْهُ أَباهُ وَإِنَّا لَفاعِلُونَ): the clause سنراود is the quoted speech. عنه: attached to نراود. The meanings of al-murāwada have already been given not long ago, so renew your acquaintance with them. أباه: a direct object. وإنا: from the conjoining of clauses. إن and its subject; the shifted lām; فاعلون is the khabar of إنا.
(وَقالَ لِفِتْيانِهِ اجْعَلُوا بِضاعَتَهُمْ فِي رِحالِهِمْ): لفتيانه: attached to قال. The clause اجعلوا is the quoted speech. بضاعتهم: a direct object. في رحالهم: in the position of the second object. There is disagreement over the meaning of putting the merchandise in their saddlebags; the nearest view is that he wanted to move them to return to him by having them recognise it when they returned to their family, which would move them to come back, since he knew that their religion did not permit them to keep it, so they would return on its account.
(لَعَلَّهُمْ يَعْرِفُونَها إِذَا انْقَلَبُوا إِلى أَهْلِهِمْ لَعَلَّهُمْ يَرْجِعُونَ): laʿalla and its subject; the clause يعرفونها is the khabar of laʿalla. إذا is an adverb for the future time. The clause انقلبوا is annexed to the adverb, and its answer is omitted, that is, "so perhaps they will return". إلى أهلهم: a preposition and its genitive noun attached to انقلبوا. laʿalla and its subject; the clause يرجعون is its khabar.

dervis-irab:63-67.t:
* I'rab:
(فَلَمَّا رَجَعُوا إِلى أَبِيهِمْ قالُوا يا أَبانا مُنِعَ مِنَّا الْكَيْلُ): the فاء is a conjunction, and لما is temporal or connective. رجعوا: a verb and an agent. إلى أبيهم: a preposition and its genitive noun attached to رجعوا. The clause قالوا has no grammatical position. يا is a vocative particle, and أبانا is the one addressed, a muḍāf. منع: a passive past verb. منا: attached to منع. الكيل: a deputy agent. They are alluding to Yūsuf's words, "فإن لم تأتوني به فلا كيل لكم عندي".
(فَأَرْسِلْ مَعَنا أَخانا نَكْتَلْ وَإِنَّا لَهُ لَحافِظُونَ): the فاء is the eloquent fāʾ (al-fāʾ al-faṣīḥa). أرسل: an imperative verb. معنا: attached to أرسل. أخانا: a direct object. نكتل: an imperfect verb, jussive in answer to the request. وإنا: inna and its subject. له: attached to حافظون. The shifted lām. حافظون: the khabar of inna.
(قالَ هَلْ آمَنُكُمْ عَلَيْهِ إِلَّا كَما أَمِنْتُكُمْ عَلى أَخِيهِ مِنْ قَبْلُ): the clause is resumptive, the answer to an implied question, as parallels to this have already occurred in many places. هل: an interrogative particle. آمنكم: an imperfect verb, a latent agent and an object. عليه: attached to آمنكم. إلا: a particle of restriction. كما أمنتكم: the kāf is an adjective of an omitted absolute object, and ما is maṣdar-forming. He means: "You said about Yūsuf, 'وإنا له لحافظون', just as you say it about his brother Binyāmīn, and then you betrayed your guarantee, so how can I trust you?" وعلى أخيه: a preposition and its genitive noun attached to أمنتكم. ومن قبل: a ḥāl, that is, "before this time".
(فَاللَّهُ خَيْرٌ حافِظاً وَهُوَ أَرْحَمُ الرَّاحِمِينَ): the فاء is the eloquent fāʾ. الله: a mubtadaʾ. خير: the khabar. حافظا: a tamyīz (specification) or a ḥāl. هو: a mubtadaʾ. أرحم الراحمين: the khabar. The meaning is that he put his trust in Allah and handed Binyāmīn over to them.
(وَلَمَّا فَتَحُوا مَتاعَهُمْ وَجَدُوا بِضاعَتَهُمْ رُدَّتْ إِلَيْهِمْ): لما is temporal or connective. فتحوا متاعهم: a verb, an agent and a direct object. ووجدوا بضاعتهم: a verb, an agent and a direct object. The clause ردت إليهم is in the position of the accusative as the second object of وجدوا.
(قالُوا يا أَبانا ما نَبْغِي): قالوا: a verb and an agent. يا أبانا: the one addressed, a muḍāf. ما: an interrogative noun in the position of the accusative as a fronted object of نبغي, that is, "what more do we seek and ask of generosity than this? Here are our goods, returned to us." al-Zajjāj said: it may be negative, that is, "there is nothing left for us to ask for"; it is also possible that نبغي is from al-baghy (transgression), that is, "we have not fabricated, so we lied about this king."
(هذِهِ بِضاعَتُنا رُدَّتْ إِلَيْنا): هذه: a mubtadaʾ. بضاعتنا: the khabar. The clause ردت إلينا is circumstantial. It is also permissible to parse بضاعتنا as a badal (substitute) from هذه, with the clause ردت إلينا as the khabar; the sentence is resumptive, introduced to clarify their words ما نبغي.
(وَنَمِيرُ أَهْلَنا وَنَحْفَظُ أَخانا وَنَزْدادُ كَيْلَ بَعِيرٍ): the واو is conjoined to an omitted clause, that is, "we shall be strengthened and helped by it, and we shall provide for our family". أهلنا: a direct object. ونحفظ أخانا: a clause conjoined to what precedes. ونزداد: also a conjoined clause. كيل بعير: a direct object of نزداد.
(ذلِكَ كَيْلٌ يَسِيرٌ): ذلك: a mubtadaʾ. كيل: the khabar. يسير: an adjective; that is, the measure of a camel-load that we shall gain is easy for the king, since he has treated us well and honoured us more than that.
(قالَ لَنْ أُرْسِلَهُ مَعَكُمْ حَتَّى تُؤْتُونِ مَوْثِقاً مِنَ اللَّهِ): لن is a particle of negation, accusative and futurity. أرسله: an imperfect verb made accusative by لن. معكم: an adverb attached to أرسله. حتى: a particle of limit and genitive. تؤتوني: an imperfect verb made accusative by an implied أن; the nūn is for protection and the first-person yāʾ is a first direct object. موثقا: a second direct object. من الله: an adjective. Swearing by Allah is made a pledge because swearing by Him is among the things by which covenants are confirmed.
(لَتَأْتُنَّنِي بِهِ إِلَّا أَنْ يُحاطَ بِكُمْ): the lām occurs in the answer to the oath indicated by his word موثقا. تأتنني: an imperfect verb, nominative by the retention of the nūn, which is dropped because of the succession of identical letters; the plural wāw, dropped because of the meeting of two quiescent letters, is the agent; the yāʾ is a direct object; the doubled nūn is for emphasis and the third nūn is the nūn of protection. Parallels to this parsing have already occurred. إلا is a particle of exception. أن and what is in its scope are an unrestricted exception (istithnāʾ mufarragh) from the most general of circumstances, that is, "you shall surely bring him to me in every circumstance except the circumstance of being encompassed"; so it is a ḥāl; or an unrestricted exception from the most general of causes, that is, "you shall not refrain from bringing him for any cause except the cause of being encompassed." The Arabs say أحيط بفلان when he perished or was on the verge of perishing. Abū Ḥayyān's wording is: "This exception is from the object of purpose (mafʿūl min ajlihi), taking into account his words لتأتنني, even though it is affirmative in wording and negative in meaning, because the meaning is 'you shall not refrain from bringing him for anything among things except that you be encompassed'. An example of what is affirmative in wording and negative in meaning is their saying أنشدك الله إلا فعلت, that is, 'I ask you by Allah only to do it'. It is not permissible that it be excepted from circumstances, being interpreted by a maṣdar standing as a ḥāl, even though an explicit maṣdar may stand as a ḥāl, so that the implied sense would be 'you shall bring him in every circumstance except encompassment', that is, 'encompassed', because they have stated explicitly that the أن that makes a verb accusative does not stand as a ḥāl, even if it is interpreted by the maṣdar which may itself stand as a ḥāl. If you make أن and the verb stand in the place of the maṣdar that stands as an adverb of time, the implied sense would be 'you shall bring him in every time except the time of being encompassed'." I say: Ibn al-Anbārī prevented that, and said in effect: "خروجنا صياح الديك is permissible, that is, at the time of the cock's crowing, but خروجنا أن يصيح الديك and خروجنا ما يصيح الديك are not permissible, even if أن and ما are maṣdar-forming, since only the explicitly stated maṣdar stands as an adverb." Ibn Jinnī allowed it to stand as an adverb just as the explicit maṣdar does, and so he allowed, in the saying of Taʾabbaṭa Sharran:
وقالوا لها لا تنكحيه فإنه ... لأول نصل أن يلاقي مجمعا
(They said to her, "Do not marry him, for he is the first blade, if he meets a gathering,")
and in the saying of Abū Dhuʾayb al-Hudhalī:
وتالله ما إن شهلة أمّ واحد ... بأوجد مني أن يهان صغيرها
(By Allah, Shahla, mother of one, is not more grief-stricken than I when her little one is humiliated,)
that أن يلاقى be taken as "the time of his meeting the gathering," and أن يهان as "the time of the humiliation of her little one." On what Ibn Jinnī allowed, it is permissible for the verse to be left out of the exceptions and for لتأتنني به to stay on its apparent affirmative sense, with no meaning of negation implied in it. [Translator's note: the source has لا تستنعون, apparently a misprint for لا تمتنعون; the translation follows the intended sense. The wording of the two verses is rendered as given.]
(فَلَمَّا آتَوْهُ مَوْثِقَهُمْ قالَ: اللَّهُ عَلى ما نَقُولُ وَكِيلٌ): the فاء is a conjunction, and لما has preceded. آتوه: a verb, an agent and a first direct object. موثقهم: a second direct object. الله: a mubtadaʾ. على ما نقول: attached to وكيل. وكيل: the khabar of الله.
(وَقالَ يا بَنِيَّ لا تَدْخُلُوا مِنْ بابٍ واحِدٍ): يا is a vocative particle. بني: the one addressed, a muḍāf, and its sign of the accusative is the yāʾ because it is attached to the sound masculine plural. لا is prohibitive. تدخلوا: an imperfect verb jussive through لا. من باب: a preposition and its genitive noun attached to تدخلوا. واحد: an adjective. He feared that they would draw attention by entering as one group and so be struck by the evil eye or suffer harm.
(وَادْخُلُوا مِنْ أَبْوابٍ مُتَفَرِّقَةٍ وَما أُغْنِي عَنْكُمْ مِنَ اللَّهِ مِنْ شَيْءٍ): وادخلوا: an imperative verb, indeclinable through the dropping of the nūn, and the wāw is the agent. من أبواب: attached to ادخلوا. متفرقة: an adjective. وما أغني: ما is negative, and أغني is an imperfect verb whose agent is latent, its implied form being "I". عنكم: attached to أغني. من الله: a ḥāl. من: a redundant preposition. شيء: genitive in form, accusative in position as a direct object.
(إِنِ الْحُكْمُ إِلَّا لِلَّهِ عَلَيْهِ تَوَكَّلْتُ وَعَلَيْهِ فَلْيَتَوَكَّلِ الْمُتَوَكِّلُونَ): إن is negative. الحكم: a mubtadaʾ. إلا: a particle of restriction. لله: the khabar. عليه: a preposition and its genitive noun attached to توكلت. وعليه: a conjoining of clause to clause. فليتوكل: the lām is the lām of command, and يتوكل is an imperfect verb jussive through the lām of command. المتوكلون: the agent.

dervis-irab:34-41.t:
* Vocabulary:
(كَيْدَهُنَّ): الكيد is applied to various meanings, among them scheming and malice, like المكيدة and الحيلة (the ruse), and that is what is meant here. It is also applied to war, to the flint's producing fire, to vomiting, to the raven's exerting itself in its cry; and كاد قاء means "he vomited", وبنفسه جاد means "he gave of himself", and "the woman menstruated"; and كاد يفعل كذا means "he was about to do such-and-such" and "he intended".

* I'rab:
(فَاسْتَجابَ لَهُ رَبُّهُ فَصَرَفَ عَنْهُ كَيْدَهُنَّ): The fāʾ is a conjunction, and استجاب is a past verb, له is attached to it and ربه is the agent; فصرف is conjoined to فاستجاب, عنه is attached to صرف, and كيدهن is a direct object. (إِنَّهُ هُوَ السَّمِيعُ الْعَلِيمُ): inna and its noun; هو is a separating pronoun (ḍamīr faṣl) or a second mubtadaʾ; السميع العليم is the khabar of inna, or of هو, and the clause is the khabar of inna. [Translator's note: the source reads «خبر ان لإن أو لهو»; translated as the sense requires: "the khabar of inna, or of hu".] (ثُمَّ بَدا لَهُمْ مِنْ بَعْدِ ما رَأَوُا الْآياتِ لَيَسْجُنُنَّهُ حَتَّى حِينٍ): ثم is a conjunction, and بدا is a past verb whose agent is a hidden element that ليسجننه explains, i.e. "it appeared to them that they should imprison him". Sībawayh said: "The agent of بدا لهم is ليسجننه, i.e. it appeared to them that they should imprison him." Al-Mubarrad said: This is a mistake, because the agent cannot be a clause; rather the agent is what بدا indicates, namely the maṣdar. The poet said:
وحق لمن أبو موسى أبوه ... يوفقه الذي نصب الجبالا
(It is right that he whose father is Abū Mūsā should be granted success by Him who set up the mountains.)
that is, وحق الحق ("it is right, the right"), so the agent was omitted because the verb indicates it; and according to Sībawayh's school the agent of حق is يوفقه, i.e. "the granting of success is right". لهم is attached to بدا; من بعد is a ḥāl; ما is maṣdarī, and it with what lies in its sphere is annexed to بعد; رأوا is a verb and an agent and الآيات is a direct object. ليسجننه: the lām is the answer to an omitted oath, on the assumption of an omitted "saying" that is accusative as a ḥāl: i.e. "it appeared to them, after they saw the signs, saying: By Allah, we shall imprison him". So the oath clause and what follows is the content of the saying (maqūl al-qawl). يسجننه is an imperfect verb, nominative by the presence of the nūn, which was omitted because of the succession of similar letters; the omitted wāw is the agent, and the doubled nūn is the heavy nūn of emphasis, but it was not in direct contact with the verb, so the verb is declined (muʿrab); the hāʾ is an accusative direct object; and حتى is a preposition of genitive and حين is in the genitive after حتى; the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to يسجننه, i.e. "until the talk of people ceases and the rumours and false reports die down". (وَدَخَلَ مَعَهُ السِّجْنَ فَتَيانِ): The wāw is a conjunction on something omitted, and دخل is a past verb; معه is an adverb of place attached to دخل; السجن is a direct object by extension (ʿalā al-ittisāʿ); and فتيان is the agent, i.e. two servants of the king, one his cupbearer and the other the keeper of his food, who had been accused of having tried to poison the king, so he ordered them to prison and they were put in prison at the very hour Yūsuf entered. (قالَ أَحَدُهُما إِنِّي أَرانِي أَعْصِرُ خَمْراً): قال is a verb and أحدهما the agent; the clause is an explanatory resumption (istinʾāf bayānī), as already mentioned; inna and its noun, and the clause أراني is its khabar; the yāʾ is the first object of أراني and the clause أعصر خمرا is in the position of the second object. The wording of Abū Ḥayyān: "The verb of dreaming (ra'ā al-ḥilmiyya) runs the course of the verbs of the heart in that its agent and its object may be two pronouns of the same referent. So in أراني there is the latent agent pronoun, and the verb is transitive to the attached pronoun while it governs an attached pronoun in the nominative, both for one referent. It is not permitted to say ضربني or أكرمني."
(وَقالَ الْآخَرُ إِنِّي أَرانِي أَحْمِلُ فَوْقَ رَأْسِي خُبْزاً تَأْكُلُ الطَّيْرُ مِنْهُ): وقال الآخر is a verb and an agent; inna and its noun, and the clause أراني is its khabar, and the clause أحمل is the second object of أراني; فوق رأسي is an adverb attached to أحمل, or to an omitted ḥāl from خبزا, because it was originally an adjective of it, and when it was put first it was parsed as a ḥāl; خبزا is a direct object, and the clause تأكل الطير منه is an adjective of خبزا. (نَبِّئْنا بِتَأْوِيلِهِ إِنَّا نَراكَ مِنَ الْمُحْسِنِينَ): an imperative verb, نا is its object and the agent is latent, "you"; وبتأويله is attached to نبئنا; inna and its noun, and the clause نراك is its khabar; ومن المحسنين is attached to نراك. (قالَ لا يَأْتِيكُما طَعامٌ تُرْزَقانِهِ إِلَّا نَبَّأْتُكُما بِتَأْوِيلِهِ قَبْلَ أَنْ يَأْتِيَكُما): لا is negative, and يأتيكما طعام is an imperfect verb, a direct object and an agent; the clause ترزقانه is an adjective of طعام; إلا is a particle of restriction; نبأتكما is a verb, an agent and a direct object, and the mīm and alif are two particles indicating the dual. [Translator's note: the source then continues «وقيل ظرف متعلق بنبأتكما», apparently referring to قبل; translated as it stands:] It is also said that [قبل] is an adverb attached to نبأتكما, and أن with what lies in its sphere is annexed to the adverb; and the clause إلا نبأتكما is an adjective of طعام or a ḥāl from it, because it has been described. (ذلِكُما مِمَّا عَلَّمَنِي رَبِّي): The demonstrative is a mubtadaʾ, ومما is the khabar, and the clause علمني is a ṣila; علمني ربي is a verb, an object and an agent. (إِنِّي تَرَكْتُ مِلَّةَ قَوْمٍ لا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِاللَّهِ وَهُمْ بِالْآخِرَةِ هُمْ كافِرُونَ):
inna and its noun, and the clause تركت is its khabar; ملة قوم is a direct object and the clause لا يؤمنون is an adjective of قوم; بالله is attached to يؤمنون; وهم is a mubtadaʾ; بالآخرة is attached to كافرون; هم is emphasis for هم, and كافرون is the khabar of هم. The clause إني تركت is either an inceptive clause or a causal one, and in both cases it has no grammatical position. (وَاتَّبَعْتُ مِلَّةَ آبائِي إِبْراهِيمَ وَإِسْحاقَ وَيَعْقُوبَ): واتبعت is conjoined to تركت, the tāʾ being its agent; ملة آبائي is a direct object; إبراهيم is a badal of آبائي, and إسحاق ويعقوب are conjoined to إبراهيم. (ما كانَ لَنا أَنْ نُشْرِكَ بِاللَّهِ مِنْ شَيْءٍ): ما is negative, كان is a defective past verb, لنا is its fronted khabar, and أن with what lies in its sphere is its fronted noun [Translator's note: the source says "fronted" for the noun, though the noun is in fact the delayed element; translated as written]; بالله is attached to نشرك; من is a redundant preposition and شيء is genitive in form, a direct object accusative in position. (ذلِكَ مِنْ فَضْلِ اللَّهِ عَلَيْنا وَعَلَى النَّاسِ): ذلك is a mubtadaʾ, ومن فضل الله is the khabar, وعلينا is attached to فضل, and وعلى الناس is conjoined to علينا. (وَلكِنَّ أَكْثَرَ النَّاسِ لا يَشْكُرُونَ): The wāw is a conjunction, ولكن and its noun, and the clause لا يشكرون is its khabar. (يا صاحِبَيِ السِّجْنِ أَأَرْبابٌ مُتَفَرِّقُونَ خَيْرٌ أَمِ اللَّهُ الْواحِدُ الْقَهَّارُ): يا is a vocative particle, and صاحبي السجن is the one addressed, annexed, with its accusative marked by the yāʾ, and السجن is muḍāf ilayhi. It is permissible that this annexation be of the kind of annexation to an adverbial (iḍāfa ilā al-ẓarf), since the original is يا صاحبي في السجن ("O two companions in the prison"); and it is permissible that it be of the kind of annexation to what resembles a direct object, the meaning being "O dwellers of the prison"; more discussion of the meaning of annexation will come in the section on Benefits. أأرباب: the hamza is for confirmatory interrogation (istifhām taqrīrī); أرباب is a mubtadaʾ, متفرقون an adjective, and خير the khabar; أم is a conjunction, and here it is the connected type (muttaṣila); والله is conjoined to أرباب, الواحد is an adjective and القهار a second adjective. (ما تَعْبُدُونَ مِنْ دُونِهِ إِلَّا أَسْماءً سَمَّيْتُمُوها أَنْتُمْ وَآباؤُكُمْ): ما is negative, and تعبدون is an imperfect verb, nominative by the presence of the nūn, with the wāw as agent; ومن دونه is a ḥāl; إلا is a particle of restriction; أسماء is a direct object, and the clause سميتموها is an adjective, the tāʾ being an agent; أنتم is emphasis for the tāʾ and آباؤكم is conjoined to the tāʾ. The author of al-Khulāṣa said:
وإن على ضمير رفع متصل ... عطفت فافصل بالضمير المنفصل
(If you conjoin to an attached nominative pronoun, then separate with the detached pronoun.)
(ما أَنْزَلَ اللَّهُ بِها مِنْ سُلْطانٍ): ما is negative, and أنزل الله is a verb and an agent; بها is attached to أنزل; من is a redundant preposition, and سلطان is genitive in form, a direct object accusative in position; the clause is an adjective or a ḥāl, because أسماء has been described. (إِنِ الْحُكْمُ إِلَّا لِلَّهِ أَمَرَ أَلَّا تَعْبُدُوا إِلَّا إِيَّاهُ): إن is negative, الحكم is a mubtadaʾ, إلا is a particle of restriction, and لله is the khabar of الحكم; the clause أمر is resumptive or a ḥāl, and the first is more precise; أن is maṣdarī and لا is negative, and تعبدوا is an imperfect verb put in the accusative by أن; أن and what follows it is accusative by removal of the preposition, attached to أمر, i.e. "He commanded you not to worship". It is also permissible that it be explicative (mufassira), in which case لا is prohibitive and تعبدوا is jussive by لا; إلا is a particle of restriction and إياه is the object of تعبدوا. (ذلِكَ الدِّينُ الْقَيِّمُ وَلكِنَّ أَكْثَرَ النَّاسِ لا يَعْلَمُونَ): ذلك is a mubtadaʾ, الدين the khabar, القيم an adjective; ولكن: the wāw is resumptive or circumstantial; ولكن and its noun, and the clause لا يعلمون is its khabar. (يا صاحِبَيِ السِّجْنِ أَمَّا أَحَدُكُما فَيَسْقِي رَبَّهُ خَمْراً): The parsing of يا صاحبي السجن has preceded; أما is a particle of condition and elaboration; أحدكما is a mubtadaʾ, the fāʾ is connective, and the clause يسقي is the khabar of أحدكما; ربه is the first direct object and خمرا the second direct object. He left the cupbearer unspecified either because he was understood, or out of dislike of stating to the baker that he was the one who would be crucified. (وَأَمَّا الْآخَرُ فَيُصْلَبُ فَتَأْكُلُ الطَّيْرُ مِنْ رَأْسِهِ): وأما الآخر is conjoined to the first أما, and الآخر is a mubtadaʾ, the fāʾ is connective, and the clause يصلب is the khabar; فتأكل الطير: the fāʾ is a conjunction, تأكل is conjoined to يصلب, and الطير is the agent of تأكل; ومن رأسه is attached to تأكل.
(قُضِيَ الْأَمْرُ الَّذِي فِيهِ تَسْتَفْتِيانِ): قضي الأمر is a passive past verb, الأمر is the deputy agent (nāʾib fāʿil), الذي is an adjective of الأمر and فيه is attached to تستفتيان.

* Rhetoric:
In His saying, the Exalted, (إِنِّي أَرانِي أَعْصِرُ خَمْراً) there is a mursal metaphor (majāz mursal) whose connection is "what will be" and "what it comes to": he named grapes "wine" because they come to be wine. One says "so-and-so cooks bricks", meaning he cooks clay until it becomes baked brick. It is also said: الخمر is literally "grapes" in the language of Ghassān, Azd and ʿUmān. It is related from al-Muʿtamir: "I met a Bedouin carrying grapes in a container and said, 'What are you carrying?' He said, 'Wine.'" On this the speech would be literal, not figurative, but the first view is preferable.

* Benefits:
The meaning of annexation (al-iḍāfa):
Annexation is, in most cases, in the sense of the lām, because it is the original, and in the sense of min frequently; of that is the annexation of a number to what is counted and of measures to what is measured, like ثلاثة الأثواب and مائة درهم, and of that too is the annexation of one number to another, like ثلاثمائة. And it is in the sense of «في» rarely. The criterion for annexation in the sense of في is that the second be a container (ẓarf) for the first, which is the muḍāf, whether time or place. Time, as in مكر الليل and تربص أربعة أشهر; place, as in «يا صاحبي السجن»: الليل is the container of the scheming, and السجن is the container of the two companions, and the implied form is مكر في الليل and صاحبين في السجن. The criterion for annexation in the sense of من is that the first, the muḍāf, be part of the second, the muḍāf ilayhi, like خاتم فضة ("a ring of silver"); do you not see that the ring is part of the genus of silver to which it is annexed, and that it is sound to predicate the muḍāf ilayhi of the muḍāf, for one says هذا الخاتم فضة ("this ring is silver"). The majority held that annexation is of only two kinds, in the sense of the lām and in the sense of min, with no third; and what gives the impression of the sense of «في» is in the sense of the lām, figuratively, the night being made a schemer and the prison a companion, because the scheming and the companionship take place in them.

dervis-irab:15-20.t:
* Vocabulary:
(أَجْمَعُوا): It is said أجمعوا الأمر and أجمعوا عليه; it is transitive by itself and with the باء, that is, they resolved upon it with firm resolve.
(سَوَّلَتْ): The root of taswīl is the shaping of a meaning in the soul together with the hope of completing it. Al-Zamakhsharī said: سولت means "made easy", from al-sūl, which is slackness. In al-Qāmūs: سولت له نفسه كذا means "he embellished it for him, made it easy for him, and made light of it for him"; it is also said that it is from al-sawal (with two fatḥas), that is, slackness of the sinew and the like, as though the one to whom it is made attractive has expended himself on what he was eager for.
(دَلْوَهُ): In al-Mukhtār: al-dalw is the bucket with which water is drawn; دلا الدلو means "he drew it up", its pattern being that of عدا; and أدلاها means "he lowered it" into the well. In al-Qāmūs: دلوت الدلو and دليتها mean "I lowered it into the well", and دلّاها means "he pulled it to bring it out". Al-dalw is feminine, and is sometimes treated as masculine.

* I'rab:
(فَلَمَّا ذَهَبُوا بِهِ وَأَجْمَعُوا أَنْ يَجْعَلُوهُ فِي غَيابَتِ الْجُبِّ) The فاء is a conjunction; the clause is conjoined to an omitted clause understood from the course of the story, its implied form being "so he sent him with them". لما is temporal or connective (rābiṭa); ذهبوا is a verb and agent, and به is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to يذهبوا; وأجمعوا is conjoined to ذهبوا, or the wāw is the wāw of ḥāl and the clause is circumstantial, with the implied "قد". أن and what is in its scope is the object of أجمعوا or is accusative by removal of the preposition; and في غيابة الجب is attached to يجعلوه. The response to لما is omitted, its implied form being "they did to him what they did of harm". (وَأَوْحَيْنا إِلَيْهِ لَتُنَبِّئَنَّهُمْ بِأَمْرِهِمْ هذا وَهُمْ لا يَشْعُرُونَ) There is disagreement about this wāw. It is said to be a conjunction, and that the revelation to Yūsuf was in the well, when he was seventeen years old or less, to reassure his heart, and it was not a revelation of prophethood. It is also said to be redundant (zāʾida), and that it is the response to لو, that is, the clause أوحينا; this is a good view if the language supported the redundancy of the wāw. إليه is attached to أوحينا. The lām is the one that prepares for an oath; لتنبئنهم is an imperfect verb, indeclinable on the fatḥa; the ـهم is a mafʿūl bihi; بأمرهم is attached to لتنبئنهم; هذا is an adjective of أمرهم; the wāw is the wāw of ḥāl; هم is a mubtadaʾ, and the clause لا يشعرون is its khabar; and the clause is circumstantial. (وَجاؤُ أَباهُمْ عِشاءً يَبْكُونَ) The wāw is a conjunction; جاءوا is a verb and agent; أباهم is a mafʿūl bihi; عشاء is an adverbial of time attached to جاء; and the clause يبكون is a ḥāl from the wāw, that is, "at the time of evening, weeping". It is said that they came in the evening only so as to be better able to make their excuse in the darkness. (قالُوا يا أَبانا إِنَّا ذَهَبْنا نَسْتَبِقُ) The clause إنا ذهبنا is the content of the saying; inna and its noun; the clause ذهبنا is the khabar of إنّ; and the clause نستبق is a ḥāl. Racing (istibāq) takes place by running, by throwing, and by shooting competition. (وَتَرَكْنا يُوسُفَ عِنْدَ مَتاعِنا فَأَكَلَهُ الذِّئْبُ) وتركنا يوسف is conjoined to ذهبنا, and the adverbial is attached to تركنا; فأكله is conjoined, the ـه is a mafʿūl bihi and الذئب the fāʿil. Thaʿlab said: "al-dhiʾb is taken from tadhaʾʾabat al-rīḥ, when the wind blows from every direction." He said: "al-dhiʾb is hamzated because it comes from every direction."
(وَما أَنْتَ بِمُؤْمِنٍ لَنا وَلَوْ كُنَّا صادِقِينَ) The wāw is a conjunction; ما is a negative in the Ḥijāzī usage; أنت is its noun; the باء is a redundant preposition, and مؤمن is genitive in form and, in position, the khabar of ما; لنا is attached to مؤمن; the wāw of ولو is a conjunction, and لو is conditional. In this place it serves to show the realization of what the preceding statement conveys of the affirmative or negative ruling under every supposed circumstance of the circumstances that accompany it in general, by introducing it upon the most remote of them from it and the one most contrary to it, so that by its holding or its being negated along with it, its holding or negation along with other circumstances becomes evident by way of priority; and none of the other circumstances is mentioned with it, it being sufficient to mention the wāw that conjoins the sentence to its counterpart opposite it, which includes all the circumstances different from it when they are multiple. كنا is كان with its noun, and صادقين is its khabar. (وَجاؤُ عَلى قَمِيصِهِ بِدَمٍ كَذِبٍ) The wāw is a conjunction; جاءوا is a verb and agent; and على قميصه is in the position of the accusative as an adverbial, as though it were said "and they came with blood upon his shirt"; this adverbial is governed by an omitted ḥāl from دم, the implied form being "they came with false blood, while it was upon his shirt". Al-Zamakhsharī disallowed that, and you will see in the section on Benefits a useful and enjoyable discussion on this subject. بدم is attached to جاءوا and كذب is an adjective; the meaning of describing the blood as "false" will come in the section on Rhetoric. (قالَ: بَلْ سَوَّلَتْ لَكُمْ أَنْفُسُكُمْ أَمْراً فَصَبْرٌ جَمِيلٌ) بل is a particle of turning away; سولت لكم أنفسكم is verb and agent; أمرا is a mafʿūl bihi; فصبر جميل is a khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, or a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is omitted, and it is sound to begin with an indefinite noun because it is qualified. (وَاللَّهُ الْمُسْتَعانُ عَلى ما تَصِفُونَ) The wāw is a conjunction; الله is a mubtadaʾ and المستعان the khabar; على ما is attached to المستعان; and the clause تصفون is a ṣila, the returning pronoun being omitted, that is, "تصفونه". (وَجاءَتْ سَيَّارَةٌ فَأَرْسَلُوا وارِدَهُمْ فَأَدْلى دَلْوَهُ) The wāw is resumptive; جاءت سيارة is verb and agent; فأرسلوا is conjoined to جاءت, the wāw is the fāʿil, and واردهم is a mafʿūl bihi, and he was a man called Mālik ibn Dhuʿr al-Khuzāʿī, to seek water for them, because the wārid is the one who goes to the water to draw for the people; فأدلى is conjoined and دلوه is a mafʿūl bihi. (قالَ يا بُشْرى هذا غُلامٌ) يا is a vocative particle, and بشرى is an indefinite noun that is addressed as a specified one: he addressed "good tidings" wherever they were, as though saying to it "Come, for this is your time"; هذا is a mubtadaʾ and غلام the khabar. It is said that he expressed it as "a boy" because of the beauty that dazzled him when he saw him. The boy is called ghulām only because it is derived from ghulma (lust), because it is the herald of desire; it is said اغتلم الشراب when the potency of the drink intensified, and اغتلمت الأمواج when the waves surged; al-ghulāma is the feminine of al-ghulām, and Abū Nuwās used to affect elegance and say of the beautiful girl "ghulāmiyya". (وَأَسَرُّوهُ بِضاعَةً وَاللَّهُ عَلِيمٌ بِما يَعْمَلُونَ) وأسروه is verb, agent and direct object, that is, they concealed him; the pronoun refers to the wārid and his companions, and it is also said: to the brothers of Yūsuf who had returned, who thought that Yūsuf had died, so they said "this is a slave who ran away from us; if you wish we will sell him to you", and Mālik ibn Dhuʿr al-Khuzāʿī bought him.
And بضاعة is accusative as a ḥāl, that is, they concealed him as merchandise for trade; al-biḍāʿa is the portion (mā buḍiʿa) of wealth set aside for trade. (وَشَرَوْهُ بِثَمَنٍ بَخْسٍ دَراهِمَ مَعْدُودَةٍ) The wāw is a conjunction; شروه is verb, agent and direct object, that is, they sold him; بثمن is attached to شروه; بخس is an adjective; دراهم is a badal from ثمن and معدودة an adjective. Describing them as countable is a kināya (metonymy) for their fewness, because a large quantity cannot be counted. (وَكانُوا فِيهِ مِنَ الزَّاهِدِينَ) كان and its noun; فيه is attached to an omitted ḥāl. Abū Ḥayyān said: "It is attached to an implied أعني, or to an omitted word indicated by من الزاهدين, or to الزاهدين, because latitude is allowed in the preposition and its genitive noun and the adverbial." And من الزاهدين is the khabar of كانوا. Ibn Hishām said: another view regarding «وكانوا فيه من الزاهدين» is that في is attached to the mentioned زاهدين; this is impossible if you take الـ to be a relative, which is the apparent reading, because what the ṣila governs does not precede the relative, so it must then be attached to an omitted أعني, or to an omitted زاهدين indicated by the mentioned one, or to the mentioned "being" to which من الزاهدين is attached; but if you take الـ to be definite, it is clear.

* Rhetoric:
Describing the blood as "false" is an exaggeration, as though it were falsehood itself, its very essence, just as one says of a liar "he is the lie itself and falsehood in person". The agent and the object are called by the maṣdar, as one says ماء سكب, that is, مسكوب (poured water); and the agent, as in His saying «إن أصبح ماؤكم غورا», that is, غائرا (sunk away). Just as they named the maṣdar by these two, they said "the intellect" (al-ʿaql) for al-maʿqūl (the reasoned), and "the skin" (al-jild) for al-majlūd (the flogged); and from this is His saying, the Exalted: «بأيكم المفتون».

* Benefits:
Does the ḥāl precede the preposition and its genitive noun?
The grammarians forbade the fronting of the ḥāl before its owner when it is genitive, as in مررت بهند جالسة, where جالسة is a ḥāl from هند, and it is not permissible to front it before it; you do not say مررت جالسة بهند. This is roughly the position of the majority, and they gave as the reason that the connection of the governing word to the ḥāl is secondary to its connection to its owner, so it is proper that if it is made transitive to its owner by means of a particle, it be made transitive to the ḥāl by that same particle; but what prevented this is that a verb is not made transitive by one particle to two things, so they made the obligation of postponement a compensation for the sharing of the particle. Al-Fārisī, Ibn Jinnī, Ibn Kaysān, Ibn Burhān and others disagreed on this and permitted fronting, citing His saying, the Exalted: «وجاءوا على قميصه بدم كذب». In reply to al-Zamakhsharī, who said it is not a ḥāl because the ḥāl of a genitive does not precede, they said: the meaning does not support putting it in the accusative as an adverbial, because the governing word of it then is جاءوا and "above" is not an adverbial; indeed it is impossible that it be an adverbial. And they cited His saying, the Exalted: «وما أرسلناك إلا كافة للناس», for كافة is a ḥāl from the genitive, which is الناس, and it has preceded its owner, which is genitive through the lām. And they cited the like of the poet's saying:
تسليت طرا عنكم بعد بينكم ... بذكراكم حتى كأنكم عندي
(I consoled myself entirely about you after your parting, by remembering you, until it is as though you were with me.) Here طرا, in the sense of "all together", is a ḥāl from the kāf and mīm, and it has preceded its owner, which is genitive through عن. Al-Zamakhsharī and those who forbid replied that this verse is a poetic necessity, or that طرا is a ḥāl from an omitted عنكم indicated by the mentioned عنكم; and that كافة in the verse is a ḥāl from the kāf in أرسلناك, and that the tāʾ is for intensification, not for the feminine. This is so; but this section does not accommodate the profusion of replies and discussions in which these scholars engaged, so what has preceded is enough for us.

* Vocabulary:
(فَصَلَتِ الْعِيرُ): it set out from the ʿArīsh of Egypt. One says faṣala min al-balad fuṣūlan when it separated from it and passed beyond its walls. In al-Mukhtār: "faṣala min al-nāḥiya means he went out, and its pattern is jalasa." The letters fāʾ and ṣād, as the first and second radicals of the word, hold a strange secret: they indicate going out and parting. One says: faṣṣa min kadhā faṣṣan and iftaṣṣa kadhā min kadhā when he extracted it and separated it, of the pattern ḍaraba; faṣṣa the wound yafiṣṣu (also of the pattern ḍaraba) means it flowed with what was in it; faṣṣa the vein means it oozed; faṣṣa the child means he cried; faṣaṣtu a thing from a thing, so infaṣṣa, i.e., I separated it so it separated; faṣaḥa yafṣaḥu (of the pattern fataḥa), the dawn to so-and-so, means it became clear to him and its light overcame him; faṣuḥa yafṣuḥu faṣāḥatan (of the pattern ẓarufa) means his language was excellent and his speech fine, so he is faṣīḥ, and faṣāḥa is the maṣdar, and also clarity and the freedom of speech from obscurity, and it is used to describe the speaker, the speech and the word; faḍaḥa yafḍaḥu (of the pattern fataḥa) faḍḥan ʿan al-amr means he feigned ignorance of it while knowing it, as if he had left its charge and cast its consequences off himself [Translator's note: the source text here has the root faḍaḥa where the context (the f-ṣ-… series) suggests a form with ṣād or ḥāʾ; translated as printed]; faṣada yafṣidu (of the pattern ḍaraba) faṣdan al-marīḍ means he opened the sick man's vein, and faṣada lahu ʿaṭāʾan means he cut a gift for him, and iftaṣada the vein means he opened it; in the proverb: "He who has been bled for is not deprived", i.e., he who obtains some of his need is not disappointed; faṣaʿa the date yafṣaʿuhā (of the pattern fataḥa) means he pressed it with two fingers until it peeled; faṣaʿa his turban from his head means he removed it; faṣaʿa a thing means he rubbed it with two fingers so that it softened and opened from what was in it; faṣama yafṣimu faṣman (of the pattern ḍaraba) the bracelet and the like means he broke it without it coming apart; faṣama a thing means he cut it; faṣama the house (passive) means it collapsed; "a handle that had been broken (fuṣimat)"; faṣā yafṣī (of the pattern ḍaraba) a thing faṣyan means he pulled it out and removed it; faṣṣā the meat min or ʿan the bone tafṣiyatan means he freed it from it and separated it; tafaṣṣā the man min the debts means he got out of them. This is among the secrets by which our noble language is distinguished.
(تُفَنِّدُونِ): al-tafnīd is ascribing to al-fand, which is senility and the loss of reason from old age. One says "shaykh mufannad", and one does not say "ʿajūz mufannada", because she was not, in her youth, possessed of judgement that could then decline in her old age. In al-Mukhtār: al-fand with two fatḥas is lying, and it is also weakness of judgement from old age; the verb is afnada; and al-tafnīd is blame and attributing weakness of judgement. In al-Qāmūs: al-fand, with vowelling of the second letter, is folly and the loss of reason through old age or illness, error in speech and opinion, and lying, like al-ifnād; and do not say "ʿajūz mufannada", because she never had judgement. Diʿbil said:
ما أكثر الناس لا بل ما أقلهم ... الله يعلم اني لم أقل فندا
إني لأغمض عيني ثم أفتحها ... على كثير ولكن لا أرى أحدا
(How many people there are — no, how few! Allah knows I have not spoken falsely. I close my eyes and open them on many, yet I see no one.)
(الْبَدْوِ): the open country. Al-badw is the flat part of the earth in which a person appears from afar, i.e., becomes visible. Al-badw is the opposite of al-ḥaḍar (settled land), and al-bādiya the opposite of al-ḥāḍira. Yaʿqūb and his sons were owners of livestock, so they lived in the bādiya. In al-Qāmūs and al-Tāj: al-badw, al-bādiya and al-badāwa are the desert, the plurals being bādiyāt and bawādin; al-badw also means the inhabitants of the desert among the nomadic Arab tribes, who are divided into several tribes. The relative adjective is badawī with sukūn on the dāl, and badawī with fatḥa on it; the feminine is badawiyya and the plural badāwī. In al-Asās: "'Laqad badawta, O so-and-so' means you settled in the desert and became a Bedouin; 'What have you to do with badāwa?'; 'the town-dweller took on Bedouin ways'. It is said: 'Where are the people?' and you say 'They have gone to the desert (badaw)', i.e., they went out to the open country; they had a few sheep which they went out to." Al-Aṣmaʿī said: al-ḥaḍāra and al-badāwa with fatḥa; Abū Zayd said: with kasra; al-ḥaḍāra is residing in the settled land and al-badāwa residing in the open desert. Al-Mutanabbī has a beautiful comparison between settled life and Bedouin life, which we record here:
كم زورة لك في الاعراب خافية ... أدهى وقد رقدوا من زورة الذيب
أزورهم وسواد الليل يشفع لي ... وأنثني وبياض الصبح يغري بي
قد وافقوا الوحش في سكنى مراتعها ... وخالقوها بتقويض وتطنيب
(How many a hidden visit of yours among the Bedouins, while they sleep, is more cunning than the wolf's visit! I visit them while the blackness of night intercedes for me, and I turn back while the whiteness of dawn incites against me. They have agreed with the wild beasts in dwelling in their pastures, and differed from them by striking and pitching tents.) He says in this verse, describing the life of the Bedouins: they live in the open country, so they follow the course of wild animals in settling in pastures, except that they have tents which they strike and pitch both in departing and in staying, while wild animals have no tents; so they differ from them in this. Then he continued his description:
ما أوجه الحضر المستحسنات به ... كأوجه البدويات الرعابيب
حسن الحضارة مجلوب بتطرية ... وفي البداوة حسن غير مجلوب
أين المعيز من الآرام ناظرة ... وغير ناظرة في الحسن والطيب
أفدى ظباء فلاة ما عرفن بها ... مضغ الكلام ولا صبغ الحواجيب
ولا برزن من الحمام مائلة ... أوراكهنّ صقيلات العراقيب
(How can the admired faces of the town equal the faces of the supple Bedouin women? The beauty of the settled is acquired by adornment, while in the desert beauty is not acquired. Where are the goats beside the white gazelles, looking or not looking, in beauty and fragrance? I would ransom the gazelles of the wilderness, who there have not known chewing of words or dyeing of eyebrows, nor emerged from the bath with swaying hips and polished heels.) By "gazelles of the wilderness" he means the Arab women, and that they are eloquent, do not chew their words, and do not dye their eyebrows as is the custom of town women; he means that their beauty is without adornment, affectation or visits to the bath, but is innate in them.
(نَزَغَ): he corrupted between us and incited. Its origin is from the rider's pricking of the animal and urging it to run. One says nazaghahu and nasaghahu when he pricked it. In al-Mukhtār: nazagha al-shayṭān baynahum means he corrupted, and its pattern is qaṭaʿa.

* I'rab:
(اذْهَبُوا بِقَمِيصِي هذا فَأَلْقُوهُ عَلى وَجْهِ أَبِي يَأْتِ بَصِيراً) An omitted element must be supplied that prepares for his words, namely that he asked them about his father and they said: "his eyes are gone", so he said: "Go with my shirt." اذهبوا is an imperative verb and agent; بقميصي may be attached to اذهبوا, the bāʾ then being for transitivity, or it may be attached to an omitted ḥāl, i.e., "go taking my shirt with you"; and هذا is an adjective, a badal or an ʿaṭf bayān; فألقوه: the fāʾ is a conjunction, and ألقوه is a verb, agent and direct object; وعلى وجه أبي is attached to ألقوه; يأت is an imperfect verb, jussive because it is the answer to the imperative, and its agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "he"; and بصيرا is a ḥāl. Al-Zamakhsharī preferred that it be a khabar of يأت, by including in it the meaning "become seeing", and the evidence for this is «فارتد بصيرا». (وَأْتُونِي بِأَهْلِكُمْ أَجْمَعِينَ) وائتوني is conjoined to اذهبوا; بأهلكم is attached to ائتوني; and أجمعين is tawkīd (emphasis) of الأهل, i.e., with your women and children. (وَلَمَّا فَصَلَتِ الْعِيرُ قالَ أَبُوهُمْ إِنِّي لَأَجِدُ رِيحَ يُوسُفَ لَوْلا أَنْ تُفَنِّدُونِ) لما is temporal or a connective; فصلت العير is a verb and agent; إن and its ism; the lām is the shifted lām; the clause أجد is the khabar of إن; ريح يوسف is a direct object; ولولا is a particle expressing prevention due to existence; أن and what is within its scope is a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is omitted, the yāʾ of the first person being omitted from تفندون for lightness and in observance of the verse-endings. The khabar is supplied as "were it not that your ascribing senility is present", and the answer to لولا is omitted, i.e., "you would have believed me". (قالُوا تَاللَّهِ إِنَّكَ لَفِي ضَلالِكَ الْقَدِيمِ) The tāʾ is the tāʾ of oath, and الله is genitive by the tāʾ of oath; the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to the verb of oath; إن and its ism; the lām is the shifted lām; في ضلالك is the khabar of إن; and القديم is an adjective. (فَلَمَّا أَنْ جاءَ الْبَشِيرُ أَلْقاهُ عَلى وَجْهِهِ فَارْتَدَّ بَصِيراً) لما is temporal or a connective, and أن is redundant (a useful discussion of it will come in the section of Benefits); جاء البشير is a verb and agent; the clause ألقاه has no position, the hāʾ being a direct object; وعلى وجهه is attached to ألقاه; فارتد: the fāʾ is a conjunction, and ارتد is a past verb whose agent is "he", and بصيرا is a ḥāl; or ارتد is a defective past verb that works like صار, and بصيرا is its khabar. (قالَ أَلَمْ أَقُلْ لَكُمْ إِنِّي أَعْلَمُ مِنَ اللَّهِ ما لا تَعْلَمُونَ) The hamza is for confirmatory interrogation; لم is a particle of negation, reversal and jussive; أقل is an imperfect verb jussive by لم, and its agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "I"; ولكم is attached to أقل; إن and its ism; the clause أعلم is its khabar; ومن الله is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to أعلم; ما is a relative noun, direct object; and the clause لا تعلمون is the ṣila. (قالُوا يا أَبانَا اسْتَغْفِرْ لَنا ذُنُوبَنا إِنَّا كُنَّا خاطِئِينَ) يا أبانا is a vocative muḍāf; استغفر is an imperative verb whose agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "you"; ولنا is attached to استغفر; ذنوبنا is a direct object; إن and its ism; the clause كنا خاطئين is the khabar of إنا; and كان and its ism, and خاطئين its khabar. (قالَ: سَوْفَ أَسْتَغْفِرُ لَكُمْ رَبِّي إِنَّهُ هُوَ الْغَفُورُ الرَّحِيمُ) The clause سوف أستغفر is the quoted speech; ولكم is attached to أستغفر; ربي is a direct object; إن and its ism; وهو is a mubtadaʾ or a separating pronoun; and الغفور الرحيم are two khabars of إن or of هو, and the nominal clause is the khabar of إن. (فَلَمَّا دَخَلُوا عَلى يُوسُفَ آوى إِلَيْهِ أَبَوَيْهِ) It is conjoined to an omitted element, its implied form being "then they set out for Egypt, and Yūsuf and his entourage went out to meet them". دخلوا is a verb and agent; وعلى يوسف is attached to دخلوا; the clause آوى has no position; واليه is attached to آوى; and أبويه is a direct object. The apparent sense is that their entering upon him was in a tent of his in the outskirts of the town, and for that reason it is conjoined. (وَقالَ ادْخُلُوا مِصْرَ إِنْ شاءَ اللَّهُ آمِنِينَ) وادخلوا مصر is a verb, agent and direct object; إن is conditional and شاء is the protasis; the apodosis is omitted because the speech indicates it, and the conditional clause is parenthetical between the ḥāl and its owner; so آمنين is a ḥāl from the wāw. (وَرَفَعَ أَبَوَيْهِ عَلَى الْعَرْشِ وَخَرُّوا لَهُ سُجَّداً) ورفع أبويه is a verb, a latent agent and a direct object; وعلى العرش is attached to رفع; خروا is a verb and agent; وله is attached to خروا; and سجدا is a ḥāl. (وَقالَ يا أَبَتِ هذا تَأْوِيلُ رُءْيايَ مِنْ قَبْلُ) The i'rab of يا أبت has already been given; هذا is a mubtadaʾ, تأويل a khabar, رؤياي a muḍāf ilayhi, and من قبل a ḥāl. (قَدْ جَعَلَها رَبِّي حَقًّا) قد is a particle of affirmation; جعلها ربي is a verb, agent and (direct object); حقا is the second object; and the clause is an implied or concurrent ḥāl. (وَقَدْ أَحْسَنَ بِي إِذْ أَخْرَجَنِي مِنَ السِّجْنِ) The wāw is a conjunction; قد is a particle of affirmation; أحسن is a past verb; وبي is attached to أحسن. Originally أحسن is made transitive with إلى, and it is sometimes made transitive with the bāʾ, as one says "asāʾa ilayhi" and "asāʾa bihi". Kuthayyir said:
أسيئي بنا أو أحسني لا ملومة ... لعزة من أعراضنا ما استحلت
(Treat us ill or well; you are not to blame; ʿAzza may deem lawful of our honour whatever she wishes.) Ibn Hishām said: its meaning is that of ending at (ghāya), i.e., "to me" (ilayya). It was also said: أحسن includes the meaning of "was kind" (laṭafa), so it is made transitive with the bāʾ, as you say "laṭafa Allāhu bika"; the bāʾ is then for attachment, because kindness is attached to and borne by the speaker. Inclusion (taḍmīn) is common and is the imbuing of a word with another meaning. وإذ is also attached to أحسن, and the clause أخرجني is annexed to it, the agent being latent and the yāʾ a direct object; ومن السجن is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to أخرجني.
(وَجاءَ بِكُمْ مِنَ الْبَدْوِ مِنْ بَعْدِ أَنْ نَزَغَ الشَّيْطانُ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَ إِخْوَتِي) بكم is attached to جاء; ومن البدو is attached to it also; ومن بعد is a ḥāl; أن and what is within its scope is annexed to the adverb; الشيطان is the agent of نزغ; وبيني is an adverb attached to نزغ; and بين is conjoined to the first adverb; and إخوتي is annexed to بين. (إِنَّ رَبِّي لَطِيفٌ لِما يَشاءُ إِنَّهُ هُوَ الْعَلِيمُ الْحَكِيمُ) إن with its ism and khabar; لما is attached to لطيف, i.e., gentle in management for the sake of it, kind; the clause يشاء is the ṣila; إنه: إن and its ism; وهو is a separating pronoun or a mubtadaʾ; and العليم الحكيم are two khabars of إن or of هو. Parallels of this have already been given. (رَبِّ قَدْ آتَيْتَنِي مِنَ الْمُلْكِ وَعَلَّمْتَنِي مِنْ تَأْوِيلِ الْأَحادِيثِ) رب is a vocative muḍāf to the omitted yāʾ of the first person, the vocative particle being omitted; قد is a particle of affirmation; آتيتني is a verb, agent and direct object; ومن الملك: من is partitive, and it with its genitive noun is an adjective of an omitted direct object, i.e., "You have given me something great of sovereignty"; it was also said to be explicative, in which case it is attached to آتيتني; وعلمتني is conjoined to آتيتني; ومن تأويل الأحاديث is attached to علمتني. (فاطِرَ السَّماواتِ وَالْأَرْضِ) It may be an adjective of رب or a badal of it, and it may be a vocative with the vocative particle omitted, and perhaps that is better; and السموات is a muḍāf ilayhi. (أَنْتَ وَلِيِّي فِي الدُّنْيا وَالْآخِرَةِ) أنت is a mubtadaʾ and وليي a khabar; في الدنيا is a ḥāl; and الآخرة is conjoined to الدنيا. (تَوَفَّنِي مُسْلِماً وَأَلْحِقْنِي بِالصَّالِحِينَ) A verb of supplication; the nūn is the nūn of protection and the yāʾ a direct object; مسلما is a ḥāl; وألحقني is conjoined to توفني; and بالصالحين is attached to ألحقني.

* Benefits:
(أَنْ) is a maṣdar particle that puts the imperfect in the accusative and is interpreted together with what is within its scope as a maṣdar, parsed according to its position. It is also lightened from أنّ, and then occurs after verbs of certainty and supposition and what resembles them; and explicative (mufassira), which occurs after a clause that has the meaning of saying without its letters, as in «فأوحينا إليه أن اصنع الفلك»; and redundant for emphasis, as in the verse «فلما أن جاء البشير». Ibn Hishām said: "The redundant أن has no meaning other than emphasis, like the other redundant particles." Ibn al-Athīr said in al-Mathal al-Sāʾir: "As for His saying «فلما أن جاء البشير ألقاه على وجهه», if one looks at the story of Yūsuf, peace be upon him, with his brothers, from when they threw him into the well until the bearer of good news came to his father, peace be upon him, one finds that there was a long delay in between, and the commentators differed over the length of that period. Had there not been a long period and a protracted interval, أن would not have been brought after لما and before the verb; rather the verse would have been: «فلما جاء البشير ألقاه على وجهه». These are subtleties and allusions that are not taken from the grammarians, because they are not their concern."
Al-Ṣalāḥ al-Ṣafadī answered Ibn al-Athīr, saying: "I say: this is among the offences of a man's admiring his own mind. Do you not see how he conceives error to be right, then begins to boast that he has obtained what the grammarians did not have? If he had looked at this fāʾ, after what does it come? Is it after His saying «فلما ذهبوا به وأجمعوا على أن يجعلوه في غيابة الجب» and the verses relating to the incident of his being thrown into the well, or does it come after His saying «اذهبوا بقميصي هذا فألقوه على وجه أبي يأت بصيرا وائتوني بأهلكم أجمعين ولما فصلت العير قال أبوهم إني لأجد ريح يوسف لولا أن تفندون، قالوا تالله انك لفي ضلالك القديم فلما أن جاء البشير ألقاه على وجهه فارتدّ بصيرا»? Ibn al-Athīr would have known that there is no delay between these two points and no long period, because the period was only the length of the distance the bearer of good news travelled from Egypt until he reached the land of Kanʿān, which is the abode of Yaʿqūb, peace be upon him, and the measure of the distance between them is twelve days or thereabouts. For this reason the grammarians said: it is redundant here. Ibn al-Athīr has other such outrageous statements against the grammarians and others, which I have answered in my book."

dervis-irab:68-73.t:
* Vocabulary:
(الحاجة): al-arab and al-lubāna. In its derivation it goes back to a single idea, namely dwelling on a thing and clinging to it, since the one who has a need is devoted to it, constantly thinking of it, dwelling on its fulfilment. The origin of (الْحاجِّ) is that it is a tree with thorns, and whatever is of this kind clings to things, as Ibn Jinnī says in al-Khaṣāʾiṣ: whatever passes by it, it catches and clings to. So the "need" was named after it by comparison with the thorny tree, as if to say: I am dwelling upon it, holding fast to its fulfilment, like this tree in drawing to itself whatever passes by or comes near. Al-ḥawjāʾ is from it, and from it the verb is conjugated: iḥtāja yaḥtāju iḥtiyājan, aḥwaja yuḥwiju, and ḥāja yaḥūju, so he is ḥāʾij.
Al-arab is from al-arba, which is a knot; ʿaqd muʾarrab means "tightened". The need is knotted in the soul of the person, going back and forth in his thought. Al-lubāna is from their saying talabbana bi-l-makān when he stayed there and kept to it, and this is the very same meaning.
This is a weighty topic which, if it becomes familiar, leads to knowing the meanings of words and picturing their referents. al-Zajjāj mentioned in his Amālī from Ibn al-Aʿrābī that al-ʿashaqa is a tree called al-lublāba, which turns green, then thin, then yellow; from that comes the derivation of al-ʿāshiq (the lover). In the lexicon: ʿashiqa bihi, like fariḥa, means he clung to it; and al-ʿishq is the love of a lover for his beloved, or it is excess of love and intensity of attachment to it. So the original material meaning is clear, and it turned into a figurative one with a deeply rooted link between it and its derivatives. al-Zajjāj also related that the origin of al-mughāzala (flirtation) is from al-idāra (turning round) and al-fatl (twisting), because it is turning someone from a matter; from it the spindle (mighzal) was named, for its turning round and the speed of its rotation, and the gazelle (ghazāl) was named ghazāl for its speed, and the sun was named ghazāla for its turning round and its speed. He gave the reason for turning from a matter in his words: "It is said ghāzala al-kalb al-ẓabya when it ran in its track and caught up with it and overpowered it and then turned away from it; from that comes flirting with women. He said: it is as if a man plays with her and she makes him hope for herself, and when he seeks to kiss her she turns away." Then, al-ghazāla may also be the feminine of al-ghazāl; it has occurred in the speech of the Arabs, in verse and prose, old and new. al-Ṣafadī denied it in his commentary on Lāmiyyat al-ʿAjam and said: it is heard only in the sense of the sun; al-Damāmīnī rejected him and cited many attestations for it, and were it not sound, the double entendre (tawriya) would not have occurred in the poet's words about the eagle:
ترى الطير والوحش في كفها ... ومنقارها ذا عظام مزاله
فلو أمكن الشمس من خوفها ... إذا طلعت ما تسمت غزاله
(You see the birds and the wild beasts in its talon, and in its beak bones, shattered. If the sun could, out of fear of it, when it rises, it would not have been called Ghazāla.)
One who goes deep in tracing the relations among words arrives at a curious doctrine and a deep secret in the origin of language and the branching of speech within it, and in this book you will see wonders from among these secrets.
