* Vocabulary:
(كِدْنا): al-kayd is originally a ruse and deception, which in relation to Allah the Exalted is impossible. It has already been stated that expressions of this kind, which give a false impression with regard to Allah the Exalted, are taken in the sense of the ends of purposes and not their beginnings. So kayd is striving in a matter of ruse and deception, and its end is to make a person fall, without his realising it, into a disagreeable matter that he has no way of averting; kayd in relation to Allah the Exalted is taken in this sense. Ibn al-Aʿrābī said: al-kayd is scheming, whether by falsehood or by truth; on this, the meaning is "thus We schemed for Yūsuf". Ibn al-Khashshāb's wording: "Kāda has another usage in which it means arāda (he wanted), and on that Abū l-Ḥasan (al-Akhfash) and others recited:
كادت وكدت وتلك خير إرادة ... لو عاد من عصر الشبيبة ما مضى
(She wanted and I wanted, and that was the best of wishes, if what had passed of the age of youth could return.)
and they took the words of the Exalted «كذلك كدنا ليوسف» (thus We planned for Yūsuf) to mean 'We willed'." [Translator's note: the source has وحسلوا, apparently a misprint for وحملوا ("and they took").]
(اسْتَيْأَسُوا): they despaired; the addition of the sīn and tāʾ is for intensification, like ʿajiba and istaʿjaba, sakhira and istaskhara.
(خَلَصُوا): they withdrew and separated from the people, alone, with no one mingling with them.
(نَجِيًّا): al-najiyy is of the pattern faʿīl in the sense of mufāʿil, like al-ʿashīr and al-khalīṭ in the sense of the associate and the mixer, as in the words of the Exalted «وقربناه نجيا» (We brought him near in confidence), that is, as a confidant (munājiyan). This usage is singular throughout; one says "they are your khalīṭ and ʿashīr", that is, your mixers and associates. Either it is because it has the form faʿīl, like ṣadīq and its class, so it is singular because it is of the pattern of verbal nouns such as al-ṣahīl, al-waḥīd and al-dhamīl; or because it is a verbal noun meaning al-tanājī, as al-najwā is said to mean.

* I'rab:
(قالُوا فَما جَزاؤُهُ إِنْ كُنْتُمْ كاذِبِينَ): the فاء is the eloquent fāʾ. ما: an interrogative noun, a mubtadaʾ. جزاؤه: the khabar. The pronoun refers to the ṣuwāʿ, that is, "what is the penalty for its theft", or the pronoun refers to the thief. إن is conditional. كنتم is the protasis. كاذبين: the khabar of kāna. The apodosis of إن is omitted, being indicated by what precedes, that is, "what is the penalty for stealing the ṣuwāʿ, or for the thief".
(قالُوا جَزاؤُهُ مَنْ وُجِدَ فِي رَحْلِهِ فَهُوَ جَزاؤُهُ): جزاؤه: a mubtadaʾ. من is conditional or relative, a second mubtadaʾ. وجد is the ṣila or the protasis. في رحله: attached to وجد. The فاء is connective on both views. هو: a mubtadaʾ. جزاؤه: a khabar. The clause فهو جزاؤه is the khabar of من, and من and what is in its scope are the khabar of the first mubtadaʾ. On this parsing the pronoun refers to the thief. It is also possible that جزاؤه is a mubtadaʾ with the hāʾ referring to the stolen object, and من وجد في رحله is its khabar, with من meaning "that which", the implied sense being "the penalty of the ṣuwāʿ is that in whose saddle it is found". It is also possible that جزاؤه is the khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, that is, "what is asked about, its penalty", that is, his enslavement is his penalty; that was the law of the house of Yaʿqūb.
(كَذلِكَ نَجْزِي الظَّالِمِينَ): كذلك: an adjective of an omitted absolute object, that is, "We requite the wrongdoers with a requital like that requital". الظالمين: a direct object; that is, it is so in our law that is established among us.
(فَبَدَأَ بِأَوْعِيَتِهِمْ قَبْلَ وِعاءِ أَخِيهِ ثُمَّ اسْتَخْرَجَها مِنْ وِعاءِ أَخِيهِ): the فاء is a conjunction. بدأ: a past verb whose agent is latent, its implied form being "he". بأوعيتهم: a preposition and its genitive noun attached to بدأ. قبل: an adverb of time attached to an omitted ḥāl. وعاء أخيه: a genitive construct. ثم is a conjunction. استخرجها: a verb, a latent agent and a direct object. The hāʾ refers to the ṣuwāʿ, since it takes both masculine and feminine, or to the siqāya because the ṣuwāʿ carries its meaning. من وعاء أخيه: attached to استخرجها.
(كَذلِكَ كِدْنا لِيُوسُفَ): that is, "in the likeness of that scheme We schemed for Yūsuf"; the kāf is an adjective of an omitted absolute object as already stated. ليوسف: attached to كدنا.
(ما كانَ لِيَأْخُذَ أَخاهُ فِي دِينِ الْمَلِكِ): ما is negative. كان is a defective past verb with a latent subject. The lām is the lām of denial (juḥūd). يأخذ: an imperfect verb made accusative by an implied أن after the lām of denial; the lām and its genitive noun are in the position of the khabar. أخاه: a direct object. في دين الملك: a ḥāl.
(إِلَّا أَنْ يَشاءَ اللَّهُ): the exception is disconnected, since taking by the king's law does not include what is meant by his words إلا أن يشاء الله, because he took him by the law of Yaʿqūb; or the exception is connected from the most general of circumstances, that is, "except in the circumstance of His will, His permission for that and His wanting it". The clause ما كان ليأخذ أخاه etc. is a reason for what Allah did of scheming for Yūsuf, or an explanation of it, and in either case has no grammatical position.
(نَرْفَعُ دَرَجاتٍ مَنْ نَشاءُ وَفَوْقَ كُلِّ ذِي عِلْمٍ عَلِيمٌ): درجات is accusative as an adverbial. من: a direct object. The clause نشاء is a ṣila. فوق: an adverb attached to an omitted fronted khabar. كل ذي علم: a genitive construct. عليم: a postponed mubtadaʾ.
(قالُوا: إِنْ يَسْرِقْ فَقَدْ سَرَقَ أَخٌ لَهُ مِنْ قَبْلُ): إن is conditional. يسرق is the protasis. The فاء is connective because the answer is accompanied by قد. سرق أخ: a verb and an agent, and the clause is in the position of the jussive as the apodosis. له: an adjective. ومن قبل: a ḥāl. They said that to disclaim the accusation that had been proved against them, clearing their own ground, meaning that this deed is not far from Binyāmīn, for his brother who died was also a thief, and "we are not on their path since they are from another mother". The historians relate that Yūsuf had stolen an idol from his mother's father, which is widely recounted in the longer works. The better view is what al-Zajjāj related, that he said: "They lied about him in what they ascribed to him", and we say that this lie is not the first of their lies.
(فَأَسَرَّها يُوسُفُ فِي نَفْسِهِ وَلَمْ يُبْدِها لَهُمْ): the فاء is a conjunction. أسرها: a verb and a direct object, and the hāʾ refers to the following statement, namely أنتم شر مكانا, so it is a pronoun used before its antecedent on the condition of explanation. يوسف: an agent. في نفسه: attached to أسرها. ولم يبدها: conjoined to أسرها. لهم: attached to يبدها.
(قالَ أَنْتُمْ شَرٌّ مَكاناً وَاللَّهُ أَعْلَمُ بِما تَصِفُونَ): أنتم: a mubtadaʾ. شر: a khabar. مكانا: a tamyīz. The clause أنتم شر مكانا is a badal from the hāʾ. It is possible for the pronoun, the hāʾ, to refer to the argument, so that the meaning is "Yūsuf concealed within himself the argument against them in their claim of theft against him and did not disclose it to them, and said: you are worse in position". والله: a mubtadaʾ. أعلم: its khabar. بما: attached to أعلم. The clause تصفون is a ṣila.
(قالُوا يا أَيُّهَا الْعَزِيزُ إِنَّ لَهُ أَباً شَيْخاً كَبِيراً): يا is a vocative particle. أيها: the one addressed, an indefinite specific noun, and the hāʾ is for alerting. العزيز: a badal. إن is a particle resembling the verb. له: its fronted khabar. شيخا: its postponed subject. كبيرا: an adjective.
(فَخُذْ أَحَدَنا مَكانَهُ إِنَّا نَراكَ مِنَ الْمُحْسِنِينَ): the فاء is the eloquent fāʾ. خذ: an imperative verb with a latent agent, its implied form being "you". أحدنا: a direct object. مكانه: an adverb of place attached to خذ. إن and its subject; the clause نراك is its khabar. من المحسنين: attached to نراك as a second object.
(قالَ مَعاذَ اللَّهِ أَنْ نَأْخُذَ إِلَّا مَنْ وَجَدْنا مَتاعَنا عِنْدَهُ): معاذ الله: accusative as a maṣdar of an omitted verb, that is, "we seek refuge in Allah". أن نأخذ: أن and what is in its scope are accusative by removal of the preposition, attached to نعوذ. إلا: a particle of restriction. من: the object of نأخذ. The clause وجدنا is a ṣila. متاعنا: the object of وجدنا. عنده: attached to an omitted word which is the second object of وجدنا, that is, "being with him".
(إِنَّا إِذاً لَظالِمُونَ): إن and its subject. إذن is an answer and a requital. The shifted lām. ظالمون is the khabar of إنا.
(فَلَمَّا اسْتَيْأَسُوا مِنْهُ خَلَصُوا نَجِيًّا): لما is temporal or connective. استيئسوا: a verb and an agent. منه: attached to استيأسوا. خلصوا: a verb and an agent. نجيا: a ḥāl from the agent of خلصوا, that is, "they withdrew in this state, conferring in private". The ḥāl is singular while its owner is plural because najiyy is singular throughout, as stated earlier under Vocabulary.
(قالَ كَبِيرُهُمْ أَلَمْ تَعْلَمُوا أَنَّ أَباكُمْ قَدْ أَخَذَ عَلَيْكُمْ مَوْثِقاً مِنَ اللَّهِ): the hamza is for affirmative interrogation (istifhām taqrīrī). لم is a particle of negation, inversion and jussive. تعلموا: an imperfect verb jussive through لم. أن and what is in its scope take the place of the two objects of تعلموا. إن and its subject; the clause قد أخذ is its khabar. عليكم: attached to أخذ. موثقا: a direct object. من الله: an adjective of موثقا.
(وَمِنْ قَبْلُ ما فَرَّطْتُمْ فِي يُوسُفَ): there are several views on the parsing of these words. The most apparent is that من قبل is a fronted khabar, and قبل is indeclinable on the ḍamma because it is cut off from annexation in wording, not in meaning, that is, "and before this". ما is maṣdar-forming, and with what follows it is a postponed mubtadaʾ; its meaning is "and before this your neglect took place". في يوسف: attached to فرطتم.
It is also possible that ما is relative, meaning "and before this, that which you neglected regarding Yūsuf of the grave offence", the position of the relative being nominative as a mubtadaʾ too. It is also possible that ما is redundant (ṣila), added to beautify the wording, so that من is attached to the verb, which is فرطتم; Abū Ḥayyān preferred this view. Ibn Hishām said: "As for his words, the Exalted, «ومن قبل ما فرطتم في يوسف», ما is either redundant, in which case من is attached to فرطتم, or maṣdar-forming, and it was said that it and its ṣila are nominative as a mubtadaʾ whose khabar is من قبل. That was refuted because the ghāyāt (words cut off from annexation) do not occur as khabars, nor as ṣilas, nor as adjectives, nor as ḥāls; Sībawayh and a group of verifiers stated that explicitly. It is difficult for them: كيف كان عاقبة الذين من قبل. It was also said that it is accusative by conjunction with أن and its ṣila, that is, 'Did you not know your father's taking of the pledge and your neglect?' On this parsing there is a separation between the conjunction and the conjoined by the adverbial, and that is forbidden."
That is what Ibn Hishām said, and it is fine, except that we do not concede that the separation is forbidden as he mentioned; rather it is permissible, as Ibn Mālik stated, and some relied for its permissibility on the words of the Exalted: «إن الله يأمركم أن تؤدوا الأمانات إلى أهلها وإذا حكمتم بين الناس أن تحكموا بالعدل». Ibn Hishām answered this objection in his marginalia on al-Tashīl, saying that the implied sense is "and He commands you, when you judge", so it is a conjoining of clauses.
The wāw in his words ومن قبل is circumstantial in any case, so the meaning is: "Did you not know that your father took from you a pledge by Allah, when you had neglected Yūsuf before?"
(فَلَنْ أَبْرَحَ الْأَرْضَ حَتَّى يَأْذَنَ لِي أَبِي): the فاء is conjoined to an implied clause, that is, "I will remain in Egypt and will not leave it". لن is a particle of negation, accusative and futurity. أبرح: an imperfect verb made accusative by لن, and its meaning is "I leave", so it is complete (tāmm); the agent of أبرح is latent, its implied form being "I". الأرض: a direct object. حتى: a particle of limit and genitive. يأذن: an imperfect verb made accusative by an implied أن after حتى. لي: attached to يأذن. أبي: an agent.
(أَوْ يَحْكُمَ اللَّهُ لِي وَهُوَ خَيْرُ الْحاكِمِينَ): أو is a conjunction. يحكم: conjoined to يأذن; it is also possible that it is made accusative by an implied أن in the answer to the negation. الله: an agent. لي: attached to يحكم. هو: a mubtadaʾ. خير الحاكمين: the khabar.

dervis-irab:25-29.t:
* I'rab:
(وَاسْتَبَقَا الْبابَ وَقَدَّتْ قَمِيصَهُ مِنْ دُبُرٍ) The wāw is a conjunction, and the clause is connected to His saying, the Exalted, ولقد همت به وهمّ بها; and His saying كذلك لنصرف etc. is a parenthetical clause brought between the two conjoined items to confirm his purity and innocence. The meaning is: "she had indeed inclined toward him, and he refused, and the two raced to the outer door, which is the way of escape"; and for that reason He used the singular after the plural, and the preposition was dropped and the verb made to reach the genitive noun directly, like وإذا كالوهم. استبقا is a past verb and the alif is the fāʿil; الباب is accusative by removal of the preposition. وقدّت قميصه: قدّ is a past verb, its fāʿil is هي, and قميصه is a mafʿūl bihi; من دبر is a ḥāl. It is possible that قدت is conjoined to واستبقا, and possible that it is a ḥāl, that is, "and she had torn", having pulled him from behind by the upper part of the shirt, from its collar, so that it tore down to its bottom. Al-qadd is cutting and splitting, and it is mostly used for what is lengthwise. Al-Nābigha said:
تقد السلوقي المضاعف نسجه ... وتوقد بالصفاح نار الحباحب
(It cuts through the Salūqī mail, doubly woven, and kindles with the flat stones the fire of al-Ḥubāḥib.) And al-qaṭṭ is used for what is crosswise. (وَأَلْفَيا سَيِّدَها لَدَى الْبابِ) وألفيا is conjoined to what preceded, and the alif is the fāʿil; سيدها means her husband (baʿl), for a woman would say to her husband "my master" because of his authority over her; it is a mafʿūl bihi; and لدى is an adverbial in the position of the accusative as a second direct object. (قالَتْ ما جَزاءُ مَنْ أَرادَ بِأَهْلِكَ سُوءاً إِلَّا أَنْ يُسْجَنَ أَوْ عَذابٌ أَلِيمٌ) ما is an interrogative noun, a mubtadaʾ; it is also possible that ما is negative, that is, "his requital is only imprisonment or a painful punishment". جزاء is the khabar and من is a muḍāf ilayhi; the clause أراد is a ṣila; بأهلك is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to أراد; سوءا is a mafʿūl bihi; إلا is a particle of restriction; and أن and what is in its scope is a badal from جزاء, that is, "except imprisonment". It is also possible that ما is negative, جزاء a mubtadaʾ and أن يسجن its khabar; أو is a conjunction, and عذاب is conjoined to the interpreted maṣdar; أليم is an adjective; and for من it is possible to be a relative or a qualified indefinite. (قالَ هِيَ راوَدَتْنِي عَنْ نَفْسِي) قال is a past verb and its fāʿil is هو, that is, Yūsuf, defending himself and declaring his innocence; هي is a mubtadaʾ and the clause راودتني its khabar; and عن نفسي is attached to راودتني. (وَشَهِدَ شاهِدٌ مِنْ أَهْلِها) The wāw is a conjunction; شهد شاهد is verb and agent; and من أهلها is an adjective of شاهد, and he was her cousin, who was in the company of her husband.
(إِنْ كانَ قَمِيصُهُ قُدَّ مِنْ قُبُلٍ فَصَدَقَتْ وَهُوَ مِنَ الْكاذِبِينَ) The condition is the content of an omitted saying, that is, "so he said"; إن is conditional; كان قميصه is كان with its noun; the clause قدّ, that is, "was torn", in the passive, is its khabar; and من قبل is attached to قدّ. فصدقت: the فاء is connective, صدقت is a past verb, and the clause is the apodosis, that is, "then her truthfulness has appeared"; هو: the wāw is circumstantial, هو is a mubtadaʾ and من الكاذبين its khabar. It is necessary to supply "قد" so that the connective فاء may validly enter; otherwise, if it were not supplied, the entry of the فاء would not be sound, because it is a past, inflected verb. (وَإِنْ كانَ قَمِيصُهُ قُدَّ مِنْ دُبُرٍ فَكَذَبَتْ وَهُوَ مِنَ الصَّادِقِينَ) It is conjoined to the first clause, and it is like it in its i'rab.
(فَلَمَّا رَأى قَمِيصَهُ قُدَّ مِنْ دُبُرٍ قالَ إِنَّهُ مِنْ كَيْدِكُنَّ) The فاء is a conjunction; لما is temporal or connective; رأى قميصه is a verb, a latent agent and an object, and the clause قدّ من دبر is circumstantial; قال is the response to لما; and inna with its noun and khabar. (إِنَّ كَيْدَكُنَّ عَظِيمٌ) inna with its noun and khabar. (يُوسُفُ أَعْرِضْ عَنْ هذا وَاسْتَغْفِرِي لِذَنْبِكِ) يوسف is the one addressed, with the vocative particle omitted; أعرض is an imperative verb and its fāʿil is أنت; عن هذا is attached to أعرض; استغفري is an imperative verb and the yāʾ is its fāʿil; and لذنبك is attached to استغفري. (إِنَّكِ كُنْتِ مِنَ الْخاطِئِينَ) inna and its noun; the clause كنت is its khabar; من الخاطئين is the khabar of كنت; and the clause is the reason for the asking of forgiveness.

* Rhetoric:
Someone may say that the pronoun «هي» is not other than a concealed one by agreement, and it is not for an absent person but for someone who is present. The answer is what al-Sirāj al-Bulqīnī said in his treatise called «Nashr al-ʿAbīr li-Ṭayy al-Ḍamīr»: the pronoun that explains the pronoun of the absent person is either stated explicitly or dispensed with by the presence of what it refers to, by the senses or by knowledge. The sensory case is like His saying «هي راودتني عن نفسي» and «يا أبت استأجره»; so Shaykh Ibn Mālik mentioned. Abū Ḥayyān followed him up, saying: it is not as he exemplified, because these two pronouns refer back to what precedes them: the pronoun in قال refers to Yūsuf, and the pronoun in هي refers to her saying «بأهلك سوءا»; and since she referred to herself by her saying «بأهلك» and did not say "to me", he referred to her by the pronoun of absence in his saying «هي راودتني», and did not address her with "you solicited me", nor point to her with "this one solicited me"; all this is in the manner of courtesy in wording and modesty in address. So he brought out the name in the pronoun of the absent person, as a courtesy toward the king and out of shyness before him. In my view what Ibn Mālik said is preferable to what Abū Ḥayyān said, because when two persons are in dispute before a judge, the claimant says to the judge "I have such-and-such against this man", and the defendant says "he knows that he has no right against me"; the pronoun in "he" is only because of the presence of what it refers to, by the senses. More of this enjoyable discussion will come when we speak of the story of his daughter Shuʿayb in Sūrat al-Qaṣaṣ. «[Translator's note: the source reads "his son Shuʿayb" (ابنه شعيب); it is translated as written, with "daughter" supplied in the sense of the context of the story; the original wording is "ibnihi Shuʿayb".]»

* Benefits:
لدى:
It is not from the wording of لدن, even though it is from its meaning, because the final letter of لدى is weak, while that of لدن is sound. They said of it لدن with fatḥa on the lām, sukūn on the dāl and kasra on the nūn, as though they found ḍamma on the dāl heavy and so put sukūn for lightness, as they said in عضد "ʿaḍd"; and since the dāl became sukūn-vowelled while the nūn is sukūn-vowelled, they put kasra on the nūn because of the meeting of two sukūns. They also said لدن with ḍamma on the dāl, sukūn on the lām and kasra on the nūn, and they dropped the nūn from لدن for lightness, saying من لد الصلاة and لد الحائط; the dropping of the nūn is not because of the meeting of two sukūns. Know that the rule for لدن is that what follows it is put in the genitive by annexation, like the rest of the adverbials, because its nūn is part of the original word, in the place of the dāl in عند, as the Exalted said «من لدن حكيم عليم»; except that among the Arabs are those who put غدوة specifically in the accusative after it. He said:
لدن غدوة حتى ألاذ بخفها ... بقية منقوص من الظل قالص
(From morning until I took shelter at her foot in the remnant of a diminished, shrunken shade.) And Dhū al-Rumma said:
لدن غدوة حتى إذا امتدت الضحى ... وحثّ القطين الشّحشحان المكلّف
(From morning until, when the forenoon had stretched out, and the diligent, eager driver urged on the residents.) He means the camel-driver, and al-qaṭīn is the plural of qāṭin (resident). Sībawayh said in this connection:
"They put غدوة in the accusative by analogy with the specification, in cases like عندي راقود خلا and جبة صوفا, and with the object in cases like هذا ضارب زيدا and قاتل بكرا." Some of them said: غدوة is put in the accusative after لدن as the khabar of an implied كان together with its noun, the implied meaning being لدن كان الوقت غدوة; and it is also permissible to put it in the nominative as the fāʿil of an omitted verb, the implied meaning being لدن كانت غدوة, that is, "came into being", كان here being complete. «[Translator's note: the source prints "عدوة" with ʿayn in this last phrase; it is translated as غدوة, evidently a misprint.]» The usual case with لدن is that it is put in the genitive with من, as in «وعلمناه من لدنا علما». When it is annexed to the first-person yāʾ, the protective nūn is obligatory with it, as in «لدني». It is annexed to a single noun, as you have seen, and to a clause, as in انتظرتك من لدن طلعت الشمس إلى أن غربت ("I waited for you from the time the sun rose until it set").

dervis-irab:81-86.t:
* Vocabulary:
(كَظِيمٌ): that is, makẓūm (suppressed): filled with grief, holding it in and not spreading it. Qatāda said: he is the one who turns his grief over in his belly and says nothing but good. In al-Miṣbāḥ: "kaẓamtu al-ghayẓ kaẓman (of the pattern ḍaraba) and kuẓūman means you held in what was in yourself of it, out of forbearance or rage." Al-Zamakhsharī said: "faʿīl in the sense of mafʿūl, by the evidence of His saying: «وهو مكظوم», from kaẓama al-siqāʾ when one ties it tight over its fullness; and al-kaẓm with fatḥa on the ẓāʾ is the outlet of the breath; one says 'he took hold of his akẓām'." The origin of this root, as the dictionaries of the language say, is from kaẓama al-baʿīr jirratahu, 'the camel held back its cud' [Translator's note: the source has the unintelligible words «از دردها» here, apparently an intrusive fragment; translated as printed, not rendered] and refrained from chewing, and "the camels spent the night kuẓūman and kawāẓim"; and "they dug a kaẓāma, a kaẓīma, kaẓāʾim". In the ḥadīth: "He came to the kaẓāma of a people and performed ablution", which is the underground channel dug from one well to another, the watering place and the trough. Ṭarafa said:
يشربن من فضلة العقار كما استوجر ماء الكظيمة الشرب جمع شروب
(They drink from the remainder of the wine-vat as the drinkers hire the water of the kaẓīma; al-shurb is the plural of shārib.) [Translator's note: the final words are in the source text as printed, mixing gloss with the verse.] From the figurative usage: kaẓama al-ghayẓ and ʿalā al-ghayẓ, and he is kāẓim; kaẓamahu al-ghayẓ wa-l-ghamm means it took hold of his breath, so he is kaẓīm and makẓūm.
(حَرَضاً): In al-Miṣbāḥ: "ḥariḍa ḥaraḍan (of the pattern taʿiba) means he was on the verge of perishing, so he is ḥaraḍ", and the singular and others are the same in it, i.e., the dual, the plural, masculine and feminine.

* I'rab:
(ارْجِعُوا إِلى أَبِيكُمْ فَقُولُوا يا أَبانا إِنَّ ابْنَكَ سَرَقَ) ارجعوا is an imperative verb and agent; والى أبيكم is attached to ارجعوا; فقولوا is conjoined to ارجعوا; ويا أبانا is a vocative muḍāf; and إن and its ism, with the clause سرق as its khabar. (وَما شَهِدْنا إِلَّا بِما عَلِمْنا وَما كُنَّا لِلْغَيْبِ حافِظِينَ) The wāw is a conjunction; ما is negative; شهدنا is a verb and agent; إلا is a particle of restriction; وبما is attached to شهدنا; the clause علمنا is the ṣila; and ما is conjoined likewise; ما is negative; كان and its ism; وللغيب is attached to حافظين; and حافظين is the khabar of كنا. (وَسْئَلِ الْقَرْيَةَ الَّتِي كُنَّا فِيها) The wāw is a conjunction; واسأل is an imperative verb whose agent is a latent pronoun, its implied form being "you"; القرية is a direct object. The asking of the village means the asking of its people, as will come in the section of Rhetoric. والتي is an adjective; the clause كنا is the ṣila; and كان and its ism, with فيها as its khabar. (وَالْعِيرَ الَّتِي أَقْبَلْنا فِيها وَإِنَّا لَصادِقُونَ) والعير is conjoined to القرية; والتي is an adjective; the clause أقبلنا is the ṣila; وفيها is attached to أقبلنا; وإنا is a conjunction, with إن and its ism; the lām is the shifted lām; and صادقون is its khabar.
(قالَ بَلْ سَوَّلَتْ لَكُمْ أَنْفُسُكُمْ أَمْراً) قال is arranged upon an omitted element, i.e., "so they returned, and he said"; بل is a particle of rectification (iḍrāb); سولت is a past verb and the tāʾ is for the feminine; ولكم is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to سولت; أنفسكم is the agent; and أمرا a direct object. (فَصَبْرٌ جَمِيلٌ عَسَى اللَّهُ أَنْ يَأْتِيَنِي بِهِمْ جَمِيعاً إِنَّهُ هُوَ الْعَلِيمُ الْحَكِيمُ) The fāʾ is a conjunction; صبر is a khabar of an omitted mubtadaʾ, i.e., "my patience (is)"; and جميل is an adjective. عسى is one of the verbs of hope; الله is its ism; and أن and what is within its scope is its khabar. وبهم is attached to يأتيني; he said "all of them" (جمع) because the lost ones had become three: Yūsuf, Binyāmīn, and the eldest of the brothers who chose to stay in Egypt. جميعا is a ḥāl. إن and its ism; وهو is a separating pronoun or a mubtadaʾ; and العليم الحكيم is the khabar of إن or of the pronoun, with the clause the khabar of إن. (وَتَوَلَّى عَنْهُمْ وَقالَ يا أَسَفى عَلى يُوسُفَ) وتولى: the wāw is a conjunction and تولى is a past verb, i.e., he turned away from them; وعنهم is attached to تولى; وقال is conjoined to تولى; ويا is a vocative particle; and أسفا is a vocative muḍāf to the yāʾ of the first person, which turned into an alif, the origin being «يا أسفي». The discussion of the vocative annexed to the yāʾ of the first person has already been given. وعلى يوسف is attached to al-asaf. He singled out Yūsuf for mention to indicate the continuing of the grief over him, and that the calamity of him was and still is fresh and green, and that his bereavement through his two brothers renewed his grief for him, because he is the foundation of his griefs and misfortunes, along the lines of Ibn al-Rūmī's saying in lamenting his middle son:
أرى أخويك الباقيين كليهما ... يكونان للأحزان أورى من الزند
(I see your two surviving brothers both of them to be, for griefs, a better kindler than the fire-stick.) Perhaps Ibn al-Rūmī observed this lofty rhetoric.
(وَابْيَضَّتْ عَيْناهُ مِنَ الْحُزْنِ فَهُوَ كَظِيمٌ) وابيضت عيناه is a verb and agent. When much weeping occurs, the tear wears away the blackness of the eye and turns it to white. ومن الحزن is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to ابيضت; فهو: the fāʾ is a conjunction, هو is a mubtadaʾ, and كظيم its khabar. (قالُوا: تَاللَّهِ تَفْتَؤُا تَذْكُرُ يُوسُفَ حَتَّى تَكُونَ حَرَضاً أَوْ تَكُونَ مِنَ الْهالِكِينَ) قالوا is a verb and agent; the tāʾ is the tāʾ of oath and the Majestic Name is genitive by the tāʾ of oath; the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to the verb of oath; and تفتأ, i.e., "you do not cease", is one of the sisters of kāna, its ism being latent, its implied form being "you"; the clause تذكر is its khabar; يوسف is a direct object; حتى is a particle of goal and genitive; تكون is accusative by an implied أن after حتى; حرضا is the khabar of تكون, and the ism of تكون is latent, its implied form being "you"; أو is a conjunction; تكون is a defective imperfect verb and its ism is "you"; and من الهالكين is its khabar.
(قالَ إِنَّما أَشْكُوا بَثِّي وَحُزْنِي إِلَى اللَّهِ) [Translator's note: in the source text the opening of this verse is cut off at the head of the line («الَ إِنَّما…») and the verse's closing words after the parsed words are cut off; the verse is restored here from the quoted words, in the manner the text itself shows.] إنما is a particle that restrains and is restrained; أشكو بثي is an imperfect verb, a latent agent and a direct object; وحزني is conjoined to بثي; وإلى الله is attached to أشكو. Al-baththu is what comes upon a person of things by which the grief of their possessor becomes so great that he cannot conceal them; so the people of the language said. It is taken from baththtuhu, i.e., I scattered it, so the misfortune was called baththan figuratively. Dhū al-Rumma said:
وقفت على ربع لميّة ناقتي ... فما زلت أبكي عنده وأخاطبه
وأسقيه حتى كاد مما أبثه ... تكمني أحجاره وملاعبه
(My she-camel stopped at Mayya's abode; I kept weeping there and addressing it, and watering it, until, from what I poured out, its stones and its playgrounds almost spoke.) [Translator's note: the second verse's last word is printed with a stray character in the source.]
(وَأَعْلَمُ مِنَ اللَّهِ ما لا تَعْلَمُونَ) [Translator's note: the opening of this quotation is cut off in the source («َ أَعْلَمُ مِنَ اللَّهِ…»); restored from the quoted text.] وأعلم is conjoined to أشكو; ومن الله is attached to أعلم, i.e., "I know of His work, His mercy and my good opinion of Him"; ما is a direct object; and the clause لا تعلمون is the ṣila.

* Rhetoric:
1- In His saying «واسأل القرية» is a mujāz mursal (loose metaphor), since what is meant is its people, and the relation is locality (maḥalliyya). Many parallels of this figure have already been given. By "the village" he meant Egypt, i.e., "send to its people and ask them for the details of this story". Likewise His saying «والعير التي أقبلنا فيها», i.e., the people of the caravan.
2- In His saying «تالله تفتأ تذكر يوسف حتى تكون حرضا» is a genuine art of rhetoric called "the harmony of the word with the meaning" (i'tilāf al-lafẓ maʿa al-maʿnā), which is the breath of life in the art and its pillar on which it stands. It is summed up in that the words of the intended meaning be in harmony with one another, with no word jarring or uneasy beside its sisters such that it could be replaced. Three things must be observed in this regard:
(a) Choice of the individual words, which is like scattered pearls, for they are selected and picked before stringing.
(b) The stringing of each word with its sister that shapes it.
(c) The purpose intended by the speech, in its various kinds. This topic has many paths and a fine route, on which many go astray, except those whose souls are lit by the light of knowledge and certainty. We shall give examples of it before taking up the verse. Among them is the saying of the Exalted «وما جعل الله لرجل من قلبين في جوفه» and the saying of the Exalted «رب إني نذرت لك ما في بطني محررا». He used al-jawf in the first and al-baṭn in the second, and did not use al-jawf in the place of al-baṭn nor al-baṭn in the place of al-jawf, although the two words are alike in meaning, both are triliteral with the same number of letters, and have the same pattern; and had he used one in place of the other, the speech would have been jarring and uneasy. On this has come the saying of al-Aʿraj in the verses of the Ḥamāsa:
نحن بنو الموت إذا الموت نزل ... لا عار بالموت إذا حم الأجل
الموت أحلى عندنا من العسل
(We are the sons of death when death descends; there is no shame in death when the appointed time is decreed. Death is sweeter to us than honey.) And Abū al-Ṭayyib al-Mutanabbī said:
إذا شئت حفت بي على كل سابح ... رجال كأن الموت في فمها شهد
(When I wish, men gather about me on every swift horse, as if death in their mouths were honeycomb.) These are two words, al-ʿasal and al-shahd, and both are fine and in use, and neither their beauty nor their use is in doubt. The word al-ʿasal occurs in the Qur'an rather than the word al-shahd, because it is finer than it; yet despite this the word al-shahd occurs in the verse of Abū al-Ṭayyib and came out finer than the word al-ʿasal in the verse of al-Aʿraj.
It befits us, to clarify this art and show its lofty characteristics, to quote a delightful passage of Ibn al-Athīr in his book al-Mathal al-Sāʾir. He said: "I have seen a group of the ignorant who, when one of them is told that this word is fine and that one ugly, deny it and say: 'All words are fine, and the one who set up the language set up nothing but what is fine.' Whoever's ignorance reaches the point of not distinguishing between the word al-ghuṣn and the word al-ʿusluj, between the word al-mudāma and the word al-isfanṭ, between the word al-sayf and the word al-khanshalīl, and between the word al-asad and the word al-fadawkas, should not be addressed or answered with a reply, but left to his own devices, as it was said: 'Leave the ignorant, even if dung is thrown in his saddlebag.' His example in this matter is no more than that of one who equates a black Zanjī woman of pitch darkness, ill-formed, with a reddened eye and a thick lip like a kidney and hair tightly curled like a raisin, with a white Roman woman tinged with red, with a smooth cheek, a kohl-darkened eye, a mouth as if strung with pearls, and a forelock like night upon morning. If a man is of such sick sight that he equates this image with that, it is not far that he has such a sickness of thought as to equate these words with those, and there is no difference between sight and hearing in this matter."
Divisions of words: in fact words are divided in usage into jazla (strong, stately) and raqīqa (tender), and each has places where its use is fine. The jazl is used in situations of hardship and thunderclaps of threat and intimidation, and the raqīq is used in describing the pangs of longing and the agony of parting. The verse before us is among the most wonderful examples of that. For when He the Glorified brought the strangest of the words of oath relative to its sisters, namely the tāʾ, since the wāw and the bāʾ circulate more on the tongues than it, He the Glorified brought the strangest forms of the defective verbs that raise nouns and put predicates in the accusative relative to its sisters, namely تفتأ, and omitted from it the particle of negation to increase the strangeness, and because the situation is not confused by affirmation, along the lines of the saying of Imruʾ al-Qays:
فقلت: يمين الله أبرح قاعدا ... ولو قطعوا رأسي لديك وأوصالي
(I said: "By Allah's oath, I shall not cease to sit, even if they cut off my head and limbs at your door.") Likewise the word «حرضا» is stranger than all its sisters among the words of perishing, so beauty of composition and of placement required that each word be placed beside a word of its kind in strangeness and usage, aiming at good neighbourliness and desiring harmony of meanings with words, so that the words are balanced in placement and proportionate in composition. More of this harmony will come in what follows.
3- Jinās (paronomasia): which is the sharing of two words in derivation. It occurred very beautifully in His saying: «يا أسفا على يوسف».

* Benefits:
1- The grammarians stipulated, for the operation of zāla (the past of yazālu, not of yazūlu), fatiʾa, bariḥa and infakka, that they be preceded by a negation, a prohibition or an invocation, with «لا» specifically in the past, or with لن in the imperfect. They stipulated that only because they carry the sense of negation, so when negation enters upon them they turn into affirmation; so the meaning of "mā zāla Zaydun qāʾiman" is "he is standing, as in the past". The negative particle may be omitted, as was given above in the i'rab and in the noble verse «تالله تفتأ تذكر يوسف»; but omission of the negative is not analogical except under three conditions: that the verb be imperfect, that it be the answer to an oath, and that the negative be «لا». Among the examples of negation after the noun is his saying:
غير منفك أسير هوى ... كل وان ليس يعتبر
(One who is not free of being a captive of passion is every slack man who does not take heed.) [Translator's note: the wording of the verse is as printed; it is somewhat obscure.] Among the examples of negation by a verb set for negation is his saying:
ليس ينفك ذا غنى واعتزاز ... كل ذي عفة مقل قنوع
(Every chaste, content man of little means does not cease to have wealth and honour.) Among the examples of negation by a verb that incidentally carries negation is his saying:
قلما يبرح اللبيب إلى ما ... يورث الحمد داعيا أو مجيبا
(The intelligent man hardly ceases, toward what brings praise, to be a caller or a responder.) For قلما has been stripped of the meaning of fewness and made into the sense of the negative ما. Among the examples of negation by a verb that necessarily entails negation is their saying: "abītu azālu astaghfiru Allāh", i.e., "lā azālu"; its basis is that whoever refuses (abā) something does not do it, and refusal necessarily entails negation. An example of prohibition is his saying:
صاح شمر ولا تزل ذاكر المو ... ت فنسيانه ضلال مبين
(O friend, gird yourself and do not cease to remember death, for forgetting it is plain error.) And an example of invocation is Dhū al-Rumma's saying:
ألا يا اسلمي يا دار مي على البلى ... ولا زال منهلّا بجرعائك القطر
(O abode of Mayy, be safe despite decay, and may the rain never cease pouring on your sandy plain.)

2- A glimpse of the imperative verb:
The command is divided into two kinds. The linguistic: it is the demand that the agent bring the action into existence externally, in the manner of superiority (istiʿlāʾ). It was also said: the requirement of an action other than refraining, in the manner of superiority. By "requirement" is meant the demand that subsists in the soul, because that is in truth the command and naming the form by it is figurative. "Other than refraining" was said to guard against prohibition; "in the manner of superiority" to guard against supplication. An objection was raised against its being inclusive: "kuff" (refrain), because it is a requirement of an action other than refraining, so this would not be a command, but it is a command, so the definition is not inclusive; and against its being exclusive: "lā takuff", because it is a requirement of an action other than refraining so it would be a command, but it is not a command, so it is not exclusive. And the technical (ṣināʿī): it is that by which this, namely the demand for bringing about the action, is effected, and that by which this is effected is the form by which the action is demanded of the agent. The imperative verb is indeclinable (mabnī) on sukūn because that is the basis of indeclinability. Its form is taken from the imperfect. When you wish to form an imperative, you drop the imperfect prefix and look at what follows it: if it is vowelled, you form the imperative on its form and vowel, so you say, for example, from yushammiru: shammir, from yudaḥriju: daḥrij, from yathibu: thib, from yaṣilu: ṣil. If what follows the imperfect prefix is sākin, you bring for it a hamzat waṣl in order to reach pronouncing the beginning of the verb sākin, so you say, for example, from yaḍribu: iḍrib, from the like of yanṭaliqu: inṭaliq, from the like of yastakhriju: istakhrij, because beginning with a sākin in pronunciation is impossible. How fine is the saying of al-Sarrāj al-Warrāq:
يا ساكنا قلبي ذكرتك قبله ... أرأيت قبلي من بدا بالساكن
وجعلته وقفا عليك وقد غدا ... متحركا بخلاف قلب الآمن
وبذا جرى الاعراب في نحو الهوى ... فإليك معذرتي فلست بلاحن
(O you who dwell in my heart, I mentioned you before it: have you seen anyone before me begin with a sākin? I made it endowed to you, though it has become mutaḥarrik, unlike the heart of the secure. So the i'rab runs in the like of passion; to you is my excuse, for I am not making a grammatical error.) It applies whether the verb is triliteral, quinqueliteral or sexiliteral. Two verbs deviate from this rule, so no hamza is introduced to them, namely khudh and kul; and for two verbs both attaching the hamza and dropping it are allowed, namely mur and sal; the Qur'an has spoken both, saying the Exalted: «سل بني إسرائيل» «واسأل القرية»; and you say "murhu bi-kadhā" and "umurhu bi-kadhā". As for the vowel of the introduced hamza: if the past is quadriliteral, it is fatḥa in the imperative, as you say from akrama: akrim [Translator's note: the source prints «أكرم» for both the past and the imperative; translated as printed]; if the third letter of the imperfect has ḍamma, it takes ḍamma in the imperative, as you say in the imperative of qatala: uqtul; and otherwise it is kasra.
3- On «بل»:
Bal: a conjunctive particle of rectification (iḍrāb) from the first and affirmation of the judgement for the second, whether that judgement is affirmative or negative. Know that iḍrāb has two meanings. One is the invalidation of the first and retraction from it, either because of a mistake or forgetfulness: you say in the affirmative, "Zayd stood, no, ʿAmr", and in the negative, "Zayd did not stand, no, ʿAmr", as if you wished to report about ʿAmr but erred and your tongue slipped to mention Zayd, so you brought bal, rectifying away from Zayd and affirming that judgement for ʿAmr. The other is its invalidation because the term of that judgement has ended, and in this sense it occurs in the Noble Book, as in His saying: «بل سولت لكم أنفسكم أمرا فصبر جميل», as if the first story ended and he took up another; and likewise His saying: «أتأتون الذكران من العالمين» then He said: «بل أنتم قوم عادون»; he did not mean that the first did not occur. An instance of this in poetry is the saying of Ruʾba ibn al-ʿAjjāj:
قلت لزير لم تصله مريمه ... هل تعرف الربع المحيل ارسمه
عفت عوافيه وطال قدمه ... بل بلد ملء الفجاج قتمه
(I said to a zīr whose Maryam did not meet him: "Do you know the abode whose traces have faded? Its remains have been effaced and its age is long." — "No, a land whose dust fills the passes.") Al-zīr, with kasra on the zāy, is the man who mixes with women and jests with them without evil, or with it; and Maryam is his female companion. In al-Qāmūs: al-maryam is the woman who loves conversation with men and does not commit fornication. The poet said:
وزائرة ليلا كما لاح بارق ... تضوّع منها للكباء عبير
فقلت لها: أهلا وسهلا أمريم؟ ... فقالت: نعم من أنت؟ قلت لها: زير
(And a night visitor, as lightning flashes, from her the fragrance of incense wafted. I said to her: "Welcome! Maryam?" She said: "Yes; who are you?" I said to her: "A zīr.")
